title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
會試錄序
臣聞天之愛人君莫大於以賢才遺之盖
賢才者致治之本君必用賢以興治平故
天為生賢使得如志以治此所謂愛君也
恭惟
皇帝陛下嗣位之初寔當興賢之歲天下賢才
欣逢
明聖莫不奮勵以求用科舉所出盖彬彬然矣
===
今年會試禮部者凡千人尚書臣濙侍郎
臣敞臣士嘉以考試官為請
上命臣直臣循其同考官則臣驥臣怡臣鈺臣叙
臣叔剛臣日恭臣愉臣璲監試則御史臣裕臣啓
其諸執事皆一時之選祗承
德意罔敢或怠拔其尤者百人而進之臣嘗
伏思
國家一統天下

今年會試禮部者凡千人尚書臣濙侍郎
臣敬臣士嘉以考試官爲請
===
上命臣直臣循其同考官則臣驥臣恬臣鉉臣叙
臣翾臣曰恭臣愉臣璲監試則御史臣裕臣啓
其諸執事皆一時之選祗承
德意罔敢或怠拔其尤者百人而進之臣嘗
伏思
國家一統天下
punctuated:
會試錄序

臣聞天之愛人君，莫大於以賢才遺之。盖賢才者，致治之本，君必用賢以興治平，故天為生賢，使得如志以治，此所謂愛君也。恭惟皇帝陛下嗣位之初，寔當興賢之歲，天下賢才欣逢明聖，莫不奮勵以求用，科舉所出，盖彬彬然矣。今年會試禮部者凡千人，尚書臣濙、侍郎臣敞、臣士嘉以考試官為請，上命臣直、臣循。其同考官則臣驥、臣怡、臣鈺、臣叙、臣叔剛、臣日恭、臣愉、臣璲，監試則御史臣裕、臣啓，其諸執事皆一時之選。祗承德意，罔敢或怠，拔其尤者百人而進之。臣嘗伏思國家一統天下，
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

Your servant has heard that in Heaven's love for a ruler of men, nothing is greater than bestowing worthy talents upon him. For worthy talents are the foundation for bringing about good governance; a ruler must employ the worthy in order to promote order and peace. Therefore, Heaven brings forth the worthy on his behalf so that he may govern according to his aspirations—this is what is meant by loving the ruler.

Reverently reflecting upon the beginning of Your Imperial Majesty's succession to the throne, it truly coincides with the year for promoting the worthy. The worthy talents of the empire joyously encounter an enlightened sage; none fail to rouse and exert themselves in seeking employment, and those produced through the civil service examinations are indeed refined and accomplished in abundance.

This year, those taking the Metropolitan Examination at the Ministry of Rites numbered a thousand in all. Minister (Shangshu) Your servant Ying [Hu Ying 胡濙], along with Vice Ministers (Shilang) Your servant Chang [Wang Chang 王敞] and Your servant Shijia [Zhang Shijia 章士嘉], petitioned for the appointment of Examiners. His Majesty commanded Your servant Zhi [Wang Zhi 王直] and Your servant Xun [Chen Xun 陳循] to serve. The Associate Examiners were Your servant Ji, Your servant Yi, Your servant Yu, Your servant Xu, Your servant Shugang, Your servant Rigong, Your servant Yu, and Your servant Sui; the Monitoring Censors (Yushi) supervising the examination were Your servant Yu and Your servant Qi; and all the various officiating personnel were the choice selections of the age. Reverently upholding Your virtuous intent, none dared be the least bit remiss, and we selected the hundred most outstanding among the candidates and presented them.

Your servant has humbly reflected that since the Dynasty unified the empire…

title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
列聖大德克享
天心天為生賢以充任使
聖仁涵育之深皆得有所成就盖自洪武庚戌
至今將二十舉矣小大之才竭忠盡節治
效之盛比隆唐虞此皆
天之所佑豈偶然哉茲當太平之世而百人者
復蒙簡拔得詣
大廷奉
===
清問盖非常之幸也自古有志之士不為少
矣孰不欲其道之行哉然而以遭遇為難
盖必大有為之君然後能急於求賢篤於
圖治
皇上以天德居天位其所以安養天民之心即
祖宗之心而大有為者也諸生由是而進膺一
命之榮列庶官之職必當思夫天之生賢
所以佑

至今將二十舉矣小大之臣竭忠盡節治
效之盛比隆唐虞此皆
天之所佑豈偶然哉茲當太平之世而百人者
復蒙簡拔得諧
大廷奉
===
清問盖非常之幸也自古有志之士不爲少
矣孰不欲其道之行哉然而以遭遇爲難
蓋必大有爲之君然後能急於求賢篤於
圖治
皇上以天德居天位其所以安養天民之心即
祖宗之心而大有爲者也諸臣由是而進膺一
命之榮列庶官之職必當思夫天之生賢
所以佑
punctuated: 列聖大德，克享天心，天為生賢，以充任使。聖仁涵育之深，皆得有所成就。盖自洪武庚戌至今，將二十舉矣。小大之才，竭忠盡節，治效之盛，比隆唐虞。此皆天之所佑，豈偶然哉！茲當太平之世，而百人者復蒙簡拔，得詣大廷，奉清問，盖非常之幸也。自古有志之士不為少矣，孰不欲其道之行哉？然而以遭遇為難，盖必大有為之君，然後能急於求賢，篤於圖治。皇上以天德居天位，其所以安養天民之心，即祖宗之心，而大有為者也。諸生由是而進，膺一命之榮，列庶官之職，必當思夫天之生賢，所以佑
translation_en: … the great virtue of the successive Sacred Emperors has been worthy of the mind of Heaven, and Heaven has on their behalf brought forth men of worth to fill offices and missions. Deeply nourished by sacred benevolence, all have been able to achieve something of note. Indeed, from the gengxu year of the Hongwu era [1370] to the present, the examinations have been held nearly twenty times. Men of talent both great and small have exhausted their loyalty and devoted their integrity, so that the flourishing efficacy of governance rivals the height of Tang [Yao] and Yu [Shun]. All of this is blessed by Heaven—how could it be by chance! Now, in an age of great peace, these one hundred men have moreover received selection and been granted leave to proceed to the Great Court and receive the Sovereign's pure inquiries—this is truly an extraordinary fortune. Since antiquity, scholars of aspiration have not been few; which of them did not wish for his Way to be put into practice? Yet finding the right opportunity and ruler has always been difficult, for there must first be a ruler of great enterprise before he can be urgent in seeking men of worth and earnest in planning for good governance. His Majesty, occupying the Heavenly throne with Heavenly virtue, holds the very mind of the Imperial Ancestors in his desire to bring peace and nourishment to Heaven's people, and is thus a ruler of great enterprise. As the scholars advance from this point to receive the honor of an official appointment and take their places among the various offices, they must surely reflect that Heaven brings forth men of worth in order to bless …

title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
國家國家設科出而用之者盖欲成治功隆
熈運夙興夜寐盡臣職所當為而無曠官
竊祿之譏使天下皆曰科舉真足以得賢
才斯善矣小錄既成因書以為序
中順大夫詹事府少詹事兼翰林院侍讀
學士王直謹序
alt_text:
國家國家設科出而用之者蓋欲成治功隆
熙運夙興夜寐盡臣職所當為而無曠官
竊祿之譏使天下皆曰科舉真足以得賢
才斯善矣小錄既成因書以為序
中順大夫詹事府少詹事兼翰林院侍讀
學士王直謹序
punctuated:
國家，國家設科，出而用之者，盖欲成治功、隆熈運。夙興夜寐，盡臣職所當為，而無曠官竊祿之譏，使天下皆曰：「科舉真足以得賢才！」斯善矣。小錄既成，因書以為序。
中順大夫、詹事府少詹事兼翰林院侍讀學士王直謹序。
translation_en:
… the dynasty, and why the dynasty establishes the examinations—and going forth to be employed by it—is surely the desire to accomplish achievements in governance and exalt the prosperous era. Rising early and retiring late, they should fulfill all that is required of a minister's office, so as to be free from the reproach of neglecting their posts and stealing their emoluments, and cause all under Heaven to say, "The civil service examinations are truly sufficient to obtain worthy talents!" Then it will be well indeed. Now that this brief record has been completed, I have written this to serve as its preface.

Respectfully prefaced by Wang Zhi 王直, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, Vice Supervisor of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent, and concurrently Academician Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy.

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the First Year of the Zhengtong Reign (1436)

Administrators of the Memorialized Crucial Examinations (Zhi gongju guan):
Hu Ying 胡濙, Grandee of the Sixteenth Class and Minister of Rites at the Auxiliary Administration (courtesy name Yuanjie 源潔, a native of Wujin County in Changzhou Prefecture, and a metropolitan graduate of the gengchen year [1400]).
Wang Shijia 王士嘉, Right Vice Minister of Rites at the Auxiliary Administration (courtesy name Daoheng 道亨, a native of Wucheng County in Shandong, and a Student of the Directorate of Education [jiansheng]).

Examiners:
Wang Zhi 王直, Grandee of the Twentieth Class, Vice Supervisor of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent, and concurrently Academician Reader-in-Waiting in the Hanlin Academy at the Auxiliary Administration (courtesy name Xingjian 行儉, a native of Taihe County in Jiangxi, and a metropolitan graduate of the jiashen year [1404]).
Chen Xun 陳循, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting in the Hanlin Academy at the Auxiliary Administration and Grandee of the Twenty-third Class (courtesy name Dezun 德遵, a native of Taihe County in Jiangxi, and a metropolitan graduate of the yiwei year [1415]).

Associate Examiners:
Wei Ji 魏驥, Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (courtesy name Zhongfang 仲房, a native of Xiaoshan County in Zhejiang, and a tribute student [gongshi] of the yiyou year [1405]).
Li Tian 黎恬, Right Admonisher of the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent (courtesy name Qianhui 潛輝, a native of Qingjiang County in Jiangxi, and a metropolitan graduate of the renchen year [1412]).
Wang Yu 王鈺, Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy at the Auxiliary Administration and Gentleman for Managing Affairs (courtesy name Mengjian 孟堅, a native of Zhuji County in Zhejiang, and a metropolitan graduate of the renchen year [1412]).
Zhou Xu 周叙, Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy at the Auxiliary Administration (courtesy name Gongxu 功叙, a native of Jishui County in Jiangxi, and a metropolitan graduate of the wuxu year [1418]).
Chen Shugang 陳叔剛, Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy at the Auxiliary Administration (a native of Min County in Fujian, and a metropolitan graduate of the xinchou year [1421]).
Sun Yuegong 孫曰恭, Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy at the Auxiliary Administration (a native of Fengcheng County in Jiangxi, and a metropolitan graduate of the jiachen year [1424]).
Ma Yu 馬愉, Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy at the Auxiliary Administration and Gentleman of the Classics (courtesy name Xinghe 性和, a native of Linqu County in Shandong, and a metropolitan graduate of the dingwei year [1427]).
Chen Sui 陳璲, Examining Editor in the Hanlin Academy at the Auxiliary Administration and Gentleman for Attendance (courtesy name Tingjia 廷嘉, a native of Linhai County in Zhejiang, and a metropolitan graduate of the xinmao year [1411]).

Monitoring Officials (Jianshi guan):
Wang Yu 王裕, Gentleman for Literature and Investigating Censor of the Guangxi Circuit at the Auxiliary Administration (courtesy name Changwen 昌問, a native of Jinxi County in Jiangxi, and a metropolitan graduate of the dingwei year [1427]).

title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
第一場
四書
堯舜帥天下以仁而民從之
克己復禮為仁一日克己復禮天下歸仁焉為
仁由己而由人乎哉
凡事豫則立不豫則廢
易
乾元者始而亨者也利貞者性情也
九五顯比王用三驅失前禽邑人不誡吉
===
極天下之賾者存乎卦鼓天下之動者存乎辭
初率其辭而揆其方既有典常苟非其人道不
虛行
書
德惟善政政在養民水火金木土穀惟修正德
利用厚生惟和九功惟叙九叙惟歌
兹率厥典奉若天命
天子惟君萬邦百官承式

乾元者始而亨者也利貞者性情也

===
書
德惟善政政在養民水火金木土穀惟修正德
利用厚生惟和九功惟叙九叙惟歌
兹率厥典奉若天命
天子惟君萬邦百官承式

punctuated:
第一場

四書
堯、舜帥天下以仁，而民從之。
克己復禮為仁。一日克己復禮，天下歸仁焉。為仁由己，而由人乎哉？
凡事豫則立，不豫則廢。

易
乾元者，始而亨者也。利貞者，性情也。
九五，顯比。王用三驅，失前禽，邑人不誡，吉。
極天下之賾者存乎卦，鼓天下之動者存乎辭。
初率其辭而揆其方，既有典常。苟非其人，道不虛行。

書
德惟善政，政在養民。水、火、金、木、土、穀，惟修；正德、利用、厚生，惟和。九功惟叙，九叙惟歌。
兹率厥典，奉若天命。
天子惟君萬邦，百官承式。
冢宰掌邦治，統百官，均四海；司徒掌邦教，敷五
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books
1. "Yao and Shun led the world with benevolence, and the people followed them." (Great Learning)
2. "To subdue oneself and return to ritual propriety is benevolence. If for a single day one can subdue oneself and return to ritual propriety, all under heaven will ascribe benevolence to him. Does the practice of benevolence depend on oneself, or does it depend on others?" (Analects)
3. "In all things, success depends on prior preparation; without prior preparation, there is failure." (Doctrine of the Mean)

Book of Changes (Yi)
1. "The Originating Power of Qian is that which begins and brings about smooth development. Advantageousness and firmness are its nature and dispositions."
2. "Nine in the fifth place: Illustrious union. In the hunt the king uses beaters on three sides only, and forgoes game that runs off in front. The citizens need no warning. Auspicious."
3. "That which probes the most complex phenomena under heaven lies in the hexagrams; that which stirs up the movements under heaven lies in the appended statements."
4. "At first, one follows the statements and ponders their direction, and there are already constant rules. Yet if it is not the right person, the Way will not operate in vain."

Book of Documents (Shu)
1. "Virtue is seen in good government, and government is tested by the nourishing of the people. There are water, fire, metal, wood, earth, and grain—these must be duly regulated; there are the rectification of the people's virtue, the conveniences of life, and the securing of abundant means of sustentation—these must be harmoniously attended to. When the nine services have been orderly accomplished, that orderly accomplishment may be sung."
2. "Thus I follow His statutes, and reverently obey the Mandate of Heaven."
3. "The Son of Heaven rules as sovereign over the myriad states, and all the officials take him as their model."
4. "The Prime Minister (Zhongzai) presides over the governance of the state, unifies the hundred officials, and brings harmony to all within the four seas; the Minister of Education (Situ) presides over the instruction of the state, disseminates the five…"

刑暴亂司空掌邦土居四民時地利
詩
似續妣祖築室百堵西南其戶爰居爰處爰笑
爰語
帝謂文王無然畔援無然歆羨誕先登于岸
嗟嗟保介維莫之春亦又何求如何新畬於皇

===

鄭伯使其弟語來盟〔桓十四年〕齊高子來盟〔閔二年〕
楚屈完來盟于師〔僖四年〕
公會王人齊侯宋公衛侯許男曹伯陳世子款
盟于洮鄭伯乞盟〔僖八年〕公會宰周公齊侯
宋子衛侯鄭伯許男曹伯于葵丘諸侯盟于
葵丘〔僖九年〕公會齊侯宋公陳侯衛侯鄭伯許
男邢侯曹伯于淮〔僖十六年〕

Five Policy Questions [lit. "Fifth" — error for "Five" (策五道)].

Question: The imperially composed books Grand Pronouncements (Da gao), Facts of Filial Piety and Obedience (Xiaoshun shishi), and Secret Merits of Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi) are the means whereby our sacred dynasty transforms and guides all under Heaven to do good. No instructions could be greater than these; if we compare them with ancient instructions, which ones can match their excellence? Goodness originates from Heaven and is a principle shared by all human beings—does it really depend upon active exertion before it exists? When extended to others without seeking recognition or demanding recompense, it is therefore called "secret merit" (yinzhi); do those who practice it extend what is inherently their own, or do they borrow it from outside? The book states that doing good will certainly reap its reward, which is indeed the natural response of principle; is its purport the same as "the family that accumulates goodness is sure to have superabundant happiness" in the Book of Changes (Yi) and "accordance with the right is auspicious" in the Book of Documents (Shu)? Among those in antiquity who did good, who surpassed Shun and Master Yan [Yan Hui]? For Shun took from others in order to do good, and whenever Master Yan attained a single good thing, he clasped it firmly to his breast. …kind of man was Yan? Whoever aspires to be like him is just like him." Shun and Yanzi may indeed be called doers of good; may we hear the reality of the rewards they received? Please speak of this for us.
Question: Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu were all sages, so their Way ought not to have differed. Yet Mencius said, "The Way of Yao and Shun was filial piety and brotherly respect, and nothing more"; that "Yu hated fine wine and loved good words"; that "Tang held fast to the Mean and employed the worthy without regard to origin"; that "King Wen looked upon the people as if they were wounded, and gazed toward the Way as though he had not yet seen it"; and that "King Wu did not treat those near to him with familiarity, nor did he forget those far away." Why did they differ like this? Was their Way really limited to these things? Or were they capable in one respect while falling short in another? When we examine other books, their virtue is praised as utterly flourishing, and former Confucians also said that in a sage nothing fails to flourish; why, then, in recounting them to instruct ten thousand generations, did Mencius single out only these points? The Duke of Zhou transmitted their Way, yet was devoted merely to putting those four matters into practice, and moreover did not touch upon Yao and Shun—why was that? Some say that the Duke of Zhou's combining the Three Kings was like Confucius's gathering the great synthesis; is this so? Was being like this enough to make him the Duke of Zhou, or is there another, ultimate explanation? The Way of the sages is what you students ought to know; set it forth in your essays.
Question: The Way is complete within the mind. Former Confucians held that within the mind there are only the four virtues of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom, and that that upon which the governance of the Two Emperors and Three Kings was founded lay nowhere outside of these. Can the manner in which they were manifested in achievements and enterprises be set forth in detail? Confucius praised Shun for governing through non-action (wuwei); could he really have set aside this Way? When later ages modeled their governance on antiquity, they invariably looked to Tang [Yao], Yu [Shun], and the Three Dynasties. Shun's governing through non-action truly cannot be surpassed; as for those who came close to it through simplicity and tranquility…

punctuated:
者，或有其人，可得聞歟？曰簡、曰靜，果堯、舜之道歟？茲欲務簡靜而道行於天下，是故仁莫大於施惠，非富不足言惠，何以能不藏而富歟？義莫大於用兵，非威不足言兵，何以能不戰而威歟？禮莫貴於和，非讓不能和，何以能不勸而讓歟？智莫貴於辨，非明不能辨，何以能不察而明歟？皆願聞其可以行於今者，試思以對。

問：兵，國之大事，古聖人用之，未嘗有文武之分。至春秋時，論將猶貴禮樂詩書，論戰則貴仁義禮信，其分為二是从[?]？武之七德，豈止於征伐歟？其後訓武有七書，果皆古書歟？或亦有非是歟？其說有合於聖賢之旨歟？借曰兵必有法，然楚、漢之世，有不肯學劔、不學古兵法者，而皆善兵，此以何法歟？又其後則有賢將、才將之別，何以異歟？槩之漢、唐，孰可為賢？孰可為才歟？今之訓武有其制，欲使皆賢且才，當何如而可？文事武備，在孔子已然，諸生當
translation_en:
… [by means of simplicity and quietude], perhaps there were such men—can we hear about them? Are what are called "simplicity" and "quietude" truly the Way of Yao and Shun? Now, if one wishes to strive for simplicity and quietude while having the Way prevail throughout the realm: therefore, in benevolence, nothing is greater than bestowing kindness, yet without wealth one cannot speak of kindness—how can one achieve wealth without hoarding? In righteousness, nothing is greater than employing troops, yet without awe-inspiring might one cannot speak of troops—how can one achieve awe-inspiring might without fighting? In ritual propriety, nothing is more valued than harmony, yet without yielding one cannot achieve harmony—how can one bring about yielding without exhortation? In wisdom, nothing is more valued than discernment, yet without clarity one cannot discern—how can one achieve clarity without prying scrutiny? In all these matters, we wish to hear what can be put into practice today. Reflect on this and reply.

Question: Military affairs are a great matter of the state. When the ancient sages employed them, there was never a division between the civil and the military. Down to the Spring and Autumn period, in discussing generals they still valued ritual, music, the Odes, and the Documents, and in discussing warfare they valued benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, and trustworthiness. When did their division into two begin [?]? As for the seven virtues of the military, how could they be limited merely to punitive expeditions? Later on, for military instruction there were the Seven Military Classics (Qishu). Are they really all ancient books, or are some among them spurious? Do their doctrines accord with the intent of the sages and worthies? Even supposing one says that military affairs must follow set methods, during the Chu-Han contendings there were those who refused to study swordsmanship or refused to study ancient military methods, and yet both excelled in warfare—what methods did they rely upon? Still later, a distinction was made between "worthy generals" and "talented generals." Wherein lies the difference? Surveying the Han and Tang dynasties as a whole, who may be considered worthy, and who may be considered talented? Today there is an established system for military instruction; if we wish to make all generals both worthy and talented, how should this be done? Having both civil affairs and military preparedness was already so with Confucius; you students must…

title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
素講之請具以對
問字書之作尚矣天地陰陽之變化聖人之道
德功業頼此以傳豈可忽哉六書之義各有
其說可得聞歟自蒼頡以來盖屢變不暇悉
論其大篆小篆隷書何自而起歟楷書之法
又作於何人歟晉人之書善矣而謂之俗書
又何歟然欲專古書有不宜於用欲專為後
人書則又謂之俗何所處焉是歟古之為史
以通書為限顧今之士奚可畧於此故相與
===
論之
alt_text:
素講之諸生具以對
問字書之作尚矣天地陰陽之變化聖人之道
德功業賴此以傳豈可忽哉六書之義各有
其說可得聞歟自蒼頡以来盖屢變不暇悉
論其大篆小篆隷書何自而起歟楷書之法
又作於何人歟晉人之書善矣而謂之俗書
又何歟然欲專古書有不宜於用欲專為後
人書則又謂之俗何所處為是歟古之為史
以通書名為限顧今之士𡚁可畧於此故相與
論之
punctuated:
素講之，請具以對。

問：字書之作尚矣。天地陰陽之變化，聖人之道德功業，頼此以傳，豈可忽哉？六書之義，各有其說，可得聞歟？自蒼頡以來，盖屢變不暇悉論，其大篆、小篆、隷書，何自而起歟？楷書之法，又作於何人歟？晉人之書善矣，而謂之俗書，又何歟？然欲專古書，有不宜於用；欲專為後人書，則又謂之俗，何所處焉是歟？古之為史，以通書為限，顧今之士奚可畧於此？故相與論之。
translation_en:
…have long studied these matters; please set forth your replies in full.

Question: The creation of script and lexicographical works is of great antiquity. The transformations of heaven, earth, yin, and yang, as well as the moral virtue and meritorious achievements of the sages, depend upon writing to be transmitted—how could it be neglected? The principles of the Six Categories of Characters (liushu) each have their own explanations; may we hear them? Since the time of Cangjie, script has undergone repeated changes too numerous to discuss in full, but from what did Greater Seal script (dazhuan), Lesser Seal script (xiaozhuan), and Clerical script (lishu) originate? And by whom were the rules of Regular script (kaishu) created? The calligraphy of the people of the Jin dynasty was excelled, yet it was called "vulgar script" (sushu)—why was that? However, if one wishes to use only ancient script, it is not suited for practical application; and if one wishes to write solely in the scripts of later generations, it is criticized as vulgar. How should one position oneself between these to be right? In antiquity, those who served as scribes (shi) were required to master character forms as a qualification; how then could scholars of today be negligent in this regard? Therefore, let us discuss this together.

title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
四書
堯舜帥天下以仁而民從之
劉定之
同考試官脩撰孫批理明詞暢不泛不畧蓋嘗
用心於四書者
考試官學士陳批明潔可取
考試官少詹事王批四書義作者多泛而雜此
作切實明快故表而出之
聖人之行於上者有其德斯人之在於下者化其德
===
蓋以身教者從理之必然也聖人帥民以仁故民無
不從之焉已之未仁而欲人之從其仁豈不難哉傳
大學者論吾身為齊治之本著曰大哉帝堯聖莫有
及之者也君哉帝舜聖莫有踰之者也堯以何道而
帥天下之民想其都俞於廟堂者非徒有是仁言而
允蹈實踐莫非此理之公也舜以何道而帥天下之
民想其宣著於區宇者非徒有是仁聲而心得躬行
莫非此德之全也民未篤於愛也堯帥之以睦族之
愛而愛非仁乎民未篤於孝也舜帥之以底豫之孝

四書

劉定之

聖人之行於上者有其德，斯人之在於下者化其德。蓋以身教者從，理之必然也。聖人帥民以仁，故民無不從之焉；已之未仁，而欲人之從其仁，豈不難哉！傳《大學》者論吾身為齊治之本，著曰：大哉帝堯，聖莫有及之者也；君哉帝舜，聖莫有踰之者也。堯以何道而帥天下之民？想其都俞於廟堂者，非徒有是仁言，而允蹈實踐，莫非此理之公也。舜以何道而帥天下之民？想其宣著於區宇者，非徒有是仁聲，而心得躬行，莫非此德之全也。民未篤於愛也，堯帥之以睦族之愛，而愛非仁乎？民未篤於孝也，舜帥之以底豫之孝，
translation_en:
The Four Books

"Yao and Shun led the world with benevolence, and the people followed them." [Great Learning, Chapter 9]

Liu Dingzhi 劉定之

Comment by Associate Examiner and Senior Compiler (xiuzhuan) Sun 孫: The reasoning is clear and the phrasing fluent, neither vague nor cursory; clearly this is someone who has devoted serious effort to the Four Books.
Comment by Examiner and Academician (xueshi) Chen 陳: Clear and concise; worthy of selection.
Comment by Examiner and Vice Supervisor of the Household (shao zhanshi) Wang 王: Most writers of expositions on the Four Books are vague andrambling, whereas this piece is concrete, lucid, and brisk; therefore we have singled it out for publication.

When the sage acting above possesses a certain virtue, the people below are transformed by that virtue. For those who teach by personal example are followed—this is the inevitable principle of things. The sages led the people with benevolence, and therefore none among the people failed to follow them; if one is not yet benevolent oneself and yet wishes others to follow one in benevolence, how could that not be difficult!

The commentator on the Great Learning (Daxue), in discussing how one's own person is the root of regulating the family and governing the state, wrote to this effect: Great indeed was Emperor Yao—in sageliness none could equal him! A true sovereign indeed was Emperor Shun—in sageliness none could surpass him! By what Way did Yao lead the people of the world? One imagines that in his harmonious deliberations in the court, he did not merely utter benevolent words, but in his sincere treading and actual practice, everything stemmed from the impartiality of this principle. By what Way did Shun lead the people of the world? One imagines that in what he manifested throughout the realm, he did not merely possess a reputation for benevolence, but in what he grasped in his heart and practiced in his person, everything was the completeness of this virtue. When the people were not yet earnest in love, Yao led them with the love that harmonizes the clan—and is love not benevolence? When the people were not yet earnest in filial piety, Shun led them with the filial piety that brought his parents to delight…

title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
而孝非仁乎盖堯舜之為此者初非有意於民之從
而但見夫圓顱方趾非一類也莫不感發於仁而取
則焉含齒戴髮非一人也莫不興起於仁而思效焉
堯之民以之於變時雍舜之時以之民恊于中其從
之之易也如形影之随其從之之速也如桴鼓之荅
所以然者本之以德則不動而化帥之以身則不言
而喻非若所好與所令之異也愚故曰聖人之行於
上者有其德斯人之在於下者化其德詎不然夫雖
然此忠恕之道也身有是仁非忠而何以之帥民非
===
恕而何曽子甞言夫子之道而喻諸忠恕此論堯舜
之仁亦歸於忠恕無非即近以明遠假粗以喻精學
者合而考之尤信
克己復禮為仁一日克己復禮天下歸仁焉為仁
由己而由人乎哉劉定之
聖人告大賢以為仁之功其效甚速而人無不與其
機甚易而人無所預盖為仁之功不外乎勝私復禮
而已然其效甚速而至大其機在我而無難也今夫

而孝非仁乎？盖堯、舜之為此者，初非有意於民之從，而但見夫圓顱方趾非一類也，莫不感發於仁而取則焉；含齒戴髮非一人也，莫不興起於仁而思效焉。堯之民以之「於變時雍」，舜之時以之「民恊于中」，其從之之易也，如形影之随；其從之之速也，如桴鼓之荅。所以然者，本之以德則不動而化，帥之以身則不言而喻，非若所好與所令之異也。愚故曰：聖人之行於上者有其德，斯人之在於下者化其德，詎不然夫！雖然，此忠恕之道也。身有是仁，非忠而何？以之帥民，非恕而何？曽子甞言夫子之道而喻諸忠恕，此論堯、舜之仁亦歸於忠恕，無非即近以明遠，假粗以喻精，學者合而考之，尤信。

「克己復禮為仁。一日克己復禮，天下歸仁焉。為仁由己，而由人乎哉？」劉定之

聖人告大賢以為仁之功，其效甚速而人無不與，其機甚易而人無所預。盖為仁之功，不外乎勝私復禮而已，然其效甚速而至大，其機在我而無難也。今夫己者，人之私欲也，己之不克，則有以害吾仁矣；禮者，
translation_en:
… and is filial piety not benevolence? For when Yao and Shun did this, they did not initially harbor any deliberate intention that the people should follow them. Yet one saw only that those with round skulls and square feet, though not of a single kind, were all without exception moved and inspired by their benevolence and took it as their model; those with teeth in their mouths and hair on their heads, though not a single person, were all without exception roused by their benevolence and sought to emulate it. By means of it, Yao's people "were transformed and became harmonious"; by means of it, in Shun's time "the people were brought into accord with the mean." How easy it was for them to follow, like a shadow following a form! How swift it was for them to follow, like a drum answering the drumstick! The reason it was so is that when governance is rooted in virtue, it transforms without action; when the people are led by personal example, they understand without words—unlike cases where what the ruler loves differs from what he commands. Therefore I say: when the sage acting above possesses that virtue, the people below are transformed by his virtue—how could it not be so! Even so, this is the Way of conscientiousness and altruism (zhongshu). To possess this benevolence in oneself—what is this if not conscientiousness? To lead the people with it—what is this if not altruism? Master Zeng (Zengzi) once spoke of the Master's Way and explained it through conscientiousness and altruism; here, in discussing the benevolence of Yao and Shun, it likewise comes back to conscientiousness and altruism. All of this is nothing other than using what is near at hand to illuminate what is distant, and borrowing the coarse to illustrate the subtle. If the student examines them together, it will be all the more convincing.

"To subdue oneself and return to ritual propriety is benevolence. If for a single day one can subdue oneself and return to ritual propriety, all under Heaven will ascribe benevolence to him. The practice of benevolence depends on oneself; does it depend on others?" By Liu Dingzhi 劉定之.

The Sage instructed the Great Worthy regarding the effort of practicing benevolence: its effect is exceedingly swift and there is no one who does not accord it to him, while its motivating pivot is exceedingly easy and others have no part in it. For the effort of practicing benevolence goes no further than overcoming selfish desires and returning to ritual propriety; yet its effect is most swift and supremely great, and its pivot lies within oneself without difficulty. Now, "oneself" refers to a person's selfish desires; if oneself is not subdued, there will be that which harms one's benevolence. "Ritual propriety" is…

title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
天理之節文也禮之不復則無以全吾仁矣克己而
欲禮之無不復復禮而求己之無可克德由是而全
理由是而熟豈非為仁之功乎然功雖在於己而其
效則著於人是故不必夫朞月之久不待夫旬時之
遠今日克復而今日人莫不與其仁矣明日克復而
明日人莫不稱其仁矣不以遠近而異不以疎戚而
殊速在於一日之頃而大及於四海之廣然效雖在
於人而其機則在於己是故己之當克我自克爾理
之當復我自復爾勇往力行之自由而他人何所致
===
其力决意用功之自斷而他人何預有其功無由人
之難而有由己之易故曰為仁之功其效甚速而人
無不與其機甚易而人無所預詎不然夫考之此章
夫子所以為顏子告也惟顏子之至明能察其由己
之幾惟顏子之至健能致其在我之决故非禮勿視
聽言動而克復之功以致不遷怒貳過而克復之效
以著三月不違何有於一日之為仁也萬世是仰何
止於天下之歸仁也使天假之以年則由大而化自
利而安也可幾矣噫

punctuated: 天理之節文也，禮之不復，則無以全吾仁矣。克己而欲禮之無不復，復禮而求己之無可克，德由是而全，理由是而熟，豈非為仁之功乎？然功雖在於己，而其效則著於人。是故不必夫朞月之久，不待夫旬時之遠，今日克復而今日人莫不與其仁矣，明日克復而明日人莫不稱其仁矣。不以遠近而異，不以疎戚而殊，速在於一日之頃，而大及於四海之廣。然效雖在於人，而其機則在於己。是故己之當克，我自克爾；理之當復，我自復爾。勇往力行之自由，而他人何所致其力？决意用功之自斷，而他人何預有其功？無由人之難，而有由己之易。故曰：為仁之功，其效甚速而人無不與，其機甚易而人無所預，詎不然夫？考之此章，夫子所以為顏子告也。惟顏子之至明，能察其由己之幾；惟顏子之至健，能致其在我之决。故非禮勿視、聽、言、動，而克復之功以致；不遷怒、貳過，而克復之效以著。三月不違，何有於一日之為仁也？萬世是仰，何止於天下之歸仁也？使天假之以年，則由大而化，自利而安也，可幾矣。噫！
translation_en:
…the regulated refinement of Heavenly Principle; if ritual propriety is not restored, there is no way to make our benevolence whole. To subdue the self while wishing that no part of ritual propriety remains unrestored, and to restore ritual propriety while seeking that nothing of the selfish self remains to be subdued—whereby virtue becomes whole and principle becomes thoroughly familiar—is this not the effort of practicing benevolence?

Yet although the effort lies within oneself, its effect is manifested among others. Therefore, it does not require the length of a full year or month, nor does it await the distance of ten days or a season. If today one subdues the self and restores ritual propriety, today there will be no one who does not acknowledge one's benevolence; if tomorrow one subdues the self and restores ritual propriety, tomorrow there will be no one who does not praise one's benevolence. It does not vary with distance or proximity, nor does it differ between the distant and the intimate; its swiftness lies within the span of a single day, while its vastness extends across the breadth of the Four Seas.

Even so, although the effect lies with others, the pivotal mechanism lies within oneself. Therefore, when the self ought to be subdued, I simply subdue it myself; when principle ought to be restored, I simply restore it myself. Since the freedom to advance bravely and practice vigorously rests with me, how could others exert their strength on my behalf? Since the resolve to set my mind and apply effort is determined by me alone, what part could others have in its achievement? There is none of the difficulty of depending on others, and all the ease of depending on oneself. Thus it is said that in the effort of practicing benevolence, its effect is most swift and there is no one who does not accord with it, while its mechanism is most easy and others have no part in it—how could this not be so?

Examining this chapter, we see that this was what the Master taught Master Yan (Yan Hui 顏回). Only through Master Yan's utmost clarity of mind could he discern the subtle mechanism that depends on oneself; only through Master Yan's utmost vigor could he carry out the decisive resolve that rests within oneself. Thus, by not looking, listening, speaking, or acting contrary to ritual propriety, his effort in subduing the self and restoring ritual propriety was brought to completion; by not transferring his anger or repeating a fault, the effect of subduing the self and restoring ritual propriety was made manifest. Since his heart did not depart from benevolence for three months at a time, what difficulty was there in practicing benevolence for a single day? Since ten thousand generations look up to him in admiration, how could it stop merely at the world's attributing benevolence to him? Had Heaven granted him more years, then proceeding from greatness to transformation, and from practicing benevolence for its benefit to resting in it naturally, would have been within reach. Alas!

title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
也是故人之来者撫之而不拒如張三面之網而得
夫禽之来者也人之去者從之而不追如開一面之
網而失夫禽之去者也其於得失之間豁然大公無
所固必而顯比之道豈不可見乎至於人之遠者在
居邑之外吾固無所期誡人之近者在居邑之中吾
亦無所期誡其於遠近之間豁然大公無所厚薄而
顯比之道豈不可知乎盖汲汲於得者患夫失煦煦
於近者忘夫遠此心之所以私而不公卽道之所以
晦而不顯心之公者道無有不顯矣道之顯者效無
===
有不吉矣人君比天下之道豈不於斯為至乎我儀圖
之文王之不殄慍不隕聞此失前禽者也武王之不
泄邇不忘遠此不誡邑者也此所以光于四方顯于
西土而公天下之大者也爻易聖人以其所承之家
法而為有天下之法故其言如此厥有旨歟
極天下之賾者存乎卦鼓天下之動者存乎辭
劉定之
盡物理者在於易之體妙事變者在於易之用盖卦
之所以盡天下之物理而為易之體爻辭所以妙

也。是故人之来者，撫之而不拒，如張三面之網而得夫禽之来者也；人之去者，從之而不追，如開一面之網而失夫禽之去者也。其於得失之間，豁然大公，無所固必，而顯比之道，豈不可見乎？至於人之遠者在居邑之外，吾固無所期誡；人之近者在居邑之中，吾亦無所期誡。其於遠近之間，豁然大公，無所厚薄，而顯比之道，豈不可知乎？盖汲汲於得者患夫失，煦煦於近者忘夫遠，此心之所以私而不公，卽道之所以晦而不顯。心之公者，道無有不顯矣；道之顯者，效無有不吉矣。人君比天下之道，豈不於斯為至乎？我儀圖之，文王之「不殄慍，不隕聞」，此「失前禽」者也；武王之「不泄邇，不忘遠」，此「不誡邑」者也。此所以「光于四方，顯于西土」，而公天下之大者也。爻《易》聖人以其所承之家法，而為有天下之法，故其言如此，厥有旨歟！

極天下之賾者存乎卦，鼓天下之動者存乎辭。
劉定之
盡物理者在於《易》之體，妙事變者在於《易》之用。盖卦之所以盡天下之物理而為《易》之體，爻辭所以妙
translation_en:
…. Therefore, those who come are comforted and not rejected, just like spreading three sides of a hunting net and catching the game that comes toward it; those who leave are allowed to go and not pursued, just like leaving one side of the net open and losing the game that runs away. Between gain and loss, one is open-minded and supremely impartial, free of obstinacy or certainty—cannot the Way of "manifestly uniting" (xianbi) be seen in this? As for those who are distant, outside one's own settlement, I naturally issue them no demands or warnings; and for those who are near, within one's own settlement, I likewise issue them no demands or warnings. Between the distant and the near, one is open-minded and supremely impartial, showing neither favoritism nor neglect—cannot the Way of "manifestly uniting" be known from this? Indeed, he who is anxious to gain fears to lose, and he who fawns upon the near forgets the distant; this is why the mind becomes selfish and partial, which is precisely why the Way becomes obscure and unmanifest. When the mind is impartial, the Way is never unmanifest; when the Way is manifest, the result is never inauspicious. Does not the ruler's Way of uniting the world reach its utmost perfection right here? As I ponder it, King Wen's "not extinguishing his wrath, yet not letting fall his renown" is an instance of "losing the game in front"; King Wu's "not being overly familiar with the near, nor forgetting the distant" is an instance of "the people of the settlement needing no warning." This is how they "shone throughout the four quarters and were manifest in the Western land," embodying the greatness of impartiality toward the whole world. The sage who composed the line statements of the Changes (Yi) took the family traditions he inherited and made them the model for possessing the world; thus his words are like this—how profound is their meaning!

"That which probes the most complex phenomena under heaven lies in the hexagrams; that which stirs the movements under heaven lies in the appended statements."
Liu Dingzhi 劉定之
Exhausting the principles of things lies in the substance of the Changes; wondrously guiding the transformations of affairs lies in the function of the Changes. For the hexagrams are that by which the principles of things under heaven are exhausted, forming the substance of the Changes, whereas the line statements are that by which the transformations of affairs [under heaven] are wondrously…

title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
下之事變而為易之用大易之書所以無不備者豈
不以此乎今夫天下之物理至賾雜而不一也聖人
以易之何者而極盡之哉觀其天地水火之象寓於
四正之卦雷風山澤之象寓於四維之卦進退之象
於剥復乎見形似之象於井鼎乎著以至於易中之
卦莫不有象而物理之賾雜無不盡於是矣盖卦象
乃易之體而豈非盡物理者在於易之體乎若夫天
下之事理至變動而不常也聖人以易之何者而鼓
動之哉觀其潜見惕躍之變則乾之爻辭有以鼓之
===
鼓罷泣歌之變則中孚爻辭有以鼓之屯之爻鼓動
其婚媾之利師之爻鼓動其征伐之宜以至於卦中
之爻莫不有辭而事理之變動無不鼓於是矣盖爻
辭乃易之用而豈非妙事變者在於易之用乎象辭
俱至體用兼該易之為易於是有全書矣然而此聖
人作易之功未至於聖人用易之妙也化裁存乎變
推行存乎通則有以用夫易矣神明存乎其人默成
存乎德行又有以妙其用矣其孰能與於此哉古之
羲文周孔所以為至也夫

punctuated: 下之事變而為易之用，大易之書所以無不備者，豈不以此乎？今夫天下之物理，至賾雜而不一也，聖人以易之何者而極盡之哉？觀其天地水火之象，寓於四正之卦；雷風山澤之象，寓於四維之卦；進退之象，於剥、復乎見；形似之象，於井、鼎乎著。以至於易中之卦，莫不有象，而物理之賾雜，無不盡於是矣。盖卦象乃易之體，而豈非盡物理者在於易之體乎？若夫天下之事理，至變動而不常也，聖人以易之何者而鼓動之哉？觀其潜、見、惕、躍之變，則乾之爻辭有以鼓之；鼓、罷、泣、歌之變，則中孚爻辭有以鼓之；屯之爻鼓動其婚媾之利，師之爻鼓動其征伐之宜。以至於卦中之爻，莫不有辭，而事理之變動，無不鼓於是矣。盖爻辭乃易之用，而豈非妙事變者在於易之用乎？象、辭俱至，體、用兼該，易之為易，於是有全書矣。然而此聖人作易之功，未至於聖人用易之妙也。化裁存乎變，推行存乎通，則有以用夫易矣；神明存乎其人，默成存乎德行，又有以妙其用矣。其孰能與於此哉？古之羲、文、周、孔所以為至也夫！
translation_en:
…the changing affairs of the world and serve as the function of the Changes (Yi). Is it not because of this that the Book of the Great Changes leaves nothing unprovided for?

Now, the principles of things in the world are supremely intricate, heterogeneous, and not uniform; by what part of the Changes do the sages exhaustively fathom them? Observe how the images of heaven, earth, water, and fire reside in the hexagrams of the four cardinal directions; how the images of thunder, wind, mountain, and marsh reside in the hexagrams of the four corners; how the images of advance and retreat are seen in Splitting Apart (Bo) and Return (Fu); and how the images of physical resemblance are manifested in the Well (Jing) and the Cauldron (Ding). Extending to all the hexagrams within the Changes, there is none without its image, and there is nothing of the intricate heterogeneity of the principles of things that is not exhausted therein. For the hexagram images are the substance of the Changes; is it not indeed the case that exhausting the principles of things lies in the substance of the Changes?

As for the principles of affairs in the world, they are supremely shifting and inconstant; by what part of the Changes do the sages rouse them into motion? Observe how the changes of lying hidden, appearing, being vigilant, and leaping up are roused by the line statements of the Creative (Qian); how the changes of beating the drum, stopping, weeping, and singing are roused by the line statements of Inner Truth (Zhongfu); how the lines of Difficulty at the Beginning (Zhun) rouse the advantage of marital alliance; and how the lines of the Army (Shi) rouse the appropriateness of punitive expeditions. Extending to all the lines within the hexagrams, there is none without its statement, and there is nothing of the shifting movements of the principles of affairs that is not roused therein. For the line statements are the function of the Changes; is it not indeed the case that marvelously directing the changing affairs lies in the function of the Changes?

When both images and statements are complete, and both substance and function are encompassed, the Changes as the Changes thereupon becomes a complete book. Yet this is the achievement of the sages in making the Changes; it has not yet reached the subtlety of the sages in using the Changes. "Transforming and tailoring lie in change; carrying out and putting into practice lie in penetration"—thus one is able to use the Changes. "Spiritual illumination lies in the person; silent accomplishment lies in virtuous conduct"—thus one is further able to bring its function to marvelous perfection. Who is capable of participating in this? This is why in antiquity Fuxi, King Wen, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius reached the ultimate!

Book of Documents (Shu): "Now follow His constant norms, and reverently accord with the Mandate of Heaven."

Zhang Zou

Comment by Associate Examiner and Senior Compiler Wang: Most essays on this topic fail to flow smoothly; only this one not only gets the principle right, its composition is also well-ordered and lucid—truly someone well-versed in the Classic.

Comment by Associate Examiner and Vice Minister Wei: Analyzing the principle through the text, he grasps the purport of Zhonghui's counsel to Tang. Commendable, commendable!

Comment by Examiner and Academician Chen: The diction and reasoning are balanced and coherent; few among the Book of Documents scripts can match it.

Comment by Examiner and Vice Supervisor of the Household Wang: On this topic, most candidates lacked clarity regarding "norms" and the "Mandate of Heaven," whereas this composition grasped it.

That the sage follows the way of constant norms is the means by which he reverently accords with the Mandate of Heaven. For constant norms are that by which Heaven gives its mandate to the sage; when the sage follows them without transgression, is this not the means by which he reverently accords with Heaven? In antiquity, after Tang the Successful had abrogated the mandate of Xia, Zhonghui composed the "Announcement" (Zhonghui zhi gao) to relieve his remorse, saying that Heaven had endowed Tang with the qualities of courage and wisdom so that he might stand as a standard to rectify the myriad states and continue the old undertakings of Yu. Since Heaven's favor toward Tang was such, how then ought Tang to act? Therefore, the social arrangements ordained by Heaven along with their norms are the constant way of governance, and were also what Yu practiced; formerly Jie had abolished them, whereas Tang initiated the repair of human relationships so that the myriad states had a standard by which to rectify themselves. title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
克綏厥猷使萬民有所取法焉人徒知湯所率循者
典常之理也而不知典常之理實天之所命也湯勇
足以有為矣而尤率循乎典常者盖典常之道天之
所出萬世不可改也湯智足以有謀矣而尤纘禹之
舊服者盖禹之舊服理之所存萬世莫能外也是則
湯之率循典常者非徒率循典常也所以奉乎天也
湯之纘禹舊服者非徒纘禹舊服也所以順乎理也
大臣舉是以為成湯告者以見天以是道托之聖人
而聖人以是道任之於己則其承天命而有天下也
===
豈不宜哉抑觀湯之伐夏雖順天應人然承堯舜禹
授受之後於心終有所不安者故仲虺之誥首言桀
逆天命而天之命湯者不可辭次言湯德足以得民
而民之歸湯者非一日末言為君艱難之道人心離
合之幾天道福善禍淫之可畏以明今之受夏非以
利己乃有無窮之恤以深慰湯而釋其慙仲虺之忠
愛可謂至矣

克綏厥猷，使萬民有所取法焉。人徒知湯所率循者，典常之理也；而不知典常之理，實天之所命也。湯勇足以有為矣，而尤率循乎典常者，盖典常之道，天之所出，萬世不可改也；湯智足以有謀矣，而尤纘禹之舊服者，盖禹之舊服，理之所存，萬世莫能外也。是則湯之率循典常者，非徒率循典常也，所以奉乎天也；湯之纘禹舊服者，非徒纘禹舊服也，所以順乎理也。大臣舉是以為成湯告者，以見天以是道托之聖人，而聖人以是道任之於己，則其承天命而有天下也，豈不宜哉？抑觀湯之伐夏，雖順天應人，然承堯、舜、禹授受之後，於心終有所不安者。故《仲虺之誥》首言桀逆天命，而天之命湯者不可辭；次言湯德足以得民，而民之歸湯者非一日；末言為君艱難之道、人心離合之幾、天道福善禍淫之可畏，以明今之受夏，非以利己，乃有無窮之恤，以深慰湯而釋其慙。仲虺之忠愛，可謂至矣。

…was able to tranquilly carry out this course, giving the myriad people something to take as their model. People merely know that what Tang followed and abided by was the principle of the constant norms, without realizing that the principle of the constant norms was in truth what Heaven had mandated. Tang's courage was sufficient to accomplish great deeds, yet he especially followed and abided by the constant norms, because the Way of the constant norms issues from Heaven and cannot be altered for ten thousand generations. Tang's wisdom was sufficient to devise great counsels, yet he especially continued the old undertakings of Yu, because the old undertakings of Yu are wherein principle resides and nothing can depart from them for ten thousand generations. Thus, Tang's following and abiding by the constant norms was not merely following and abiding by the constant norms; it was the means by which he revered Heaven. Tang's continuing the old undertakings of Yu was not merely continuing the old undertakings of Yu; it was the means by which he complied with principle. The great minister raised these points to advise Cheng Tang in order to show that since Heaven entrusted this Way to the sage, and the sage took this Way upon himself as his own responsibility, how could his receiving the Mandate of Heaven and possessing the empire be anything less than fitting?

Moreover, when we observe Tang's punitive expedition against Xia, although it complied with Heaven and responded to the people, coming after the peaceful transfers of rule among Yao, Shun, and Yu, in his heart he ultimately felt a sense of unease. Therefore, the "Announcement of Zhonghui" (Zhonghui zhi gao) first declares that Jie defied the Mandate of Heaven and that Heaven's mandate to Tang could not be declined; next it states that Tang's virtue was sufficient to win the people and that the people's turning their allegiance to Tang had not happened in a single day; and finally it speaks of the arduous Way of being a ruler, the subtle triggers by which the people's hearts are lost or won, and the awesomeness of the Way of Heaven in blessing the good and bringing calamity upon the licentious—so as to make clear that taking over from Xia now was not for self-benefit, but entailed boundless solicitudinous care, thereby deeply consoling Tang and relieving his shame. Zhonghui's loyalty and devotion can truly be called supreme.

Comment by Associate Examiner, Vice Minister Wei: Although the Prime Minister (Zhongzai) is ranked among the Six Ministers, he has authority to oversee the affairs of the other five ministers; this composition deeply grasps the purport of the passage.

Comment by Examiner, Vice Supervisor of the Household Wang: It captures the intention behind the establishment of offices in the completed Zhou dynasty, vividly revealing the spirit of its achievement of good governance.

Aworthy ruler establishes offices to assist in the work of Heaven: he who exercises overall governance bears a heavy responsibility, while those who share in the governance hold specialized charges. Now, in planning for good governance, nothing comes before establishing offices, and in establishing offices, nothing is more essential than the Six Ministers. The responsibility of him who exercises overall governance must indeed be heavy, and how could the charges of those who share in the governance not be specialized? In antiquity, when King Cheng of Zhou rectified the governing officials, having first established the Three Dukes and Three Solitaries, he further instituted the Six Ministers thereafter. Among the Six Ministers, none is greater than the Prime Minister (Zhongzai). The Prime Minister is in fact the Minister of the Office of Heaven. Since he takes charge of the governance of the states of the realm, he serves as the chief of the governing officials, internally unifying the hundred officials and externally bringing equilibrium to all within the four seas. From the other five ministers down to the managers of affairs and the multitudinous petty officers, he must supervise and hold them together so that they are brought into unity; from the royal court out to the Man and Yi tribes and the garrison and frontier domains, he must regulate and harmonize them so that they attain balance. 徒以掌之司徒曰地官卿既掌國之敎化則夫五典
出於天得以敷其敎於民兆民處於下使之順其化
於上敎化莫先於禮樂故立宗伯以掌之宗伯曰春
官卿既掌國之典禮則夫天神地祇人鬼之事當治
之以直清上下尊卑等列之分當和之以秩序敎化禮
樂既以興行豈無弗率訓典者哉大者加以甲兵故
邦政掌以司馬司馬非夏官卿乎由是六師有統詰
戒兵而奮武烈者無擾也邦國用平强凌弱而衆暴
寡者有警也小者施以刑罰故邦禁掌以司宼司宼
===
非秋官卿乎於是姦慝隱而難知者窮詰以求其情
暴亂顯而易見者刑戮以正其罪姦慝暴亂既去民
不可以不奠故立司空於後以主國之空土司空曰
冬官卿士農工賈之雜處俾有以遂其安居作訛成
易之屢遷俾有以興其地利六卿於是乎備萬事於
是乎舉成周建官之制孰有要於此哉抑嘗論之冢

統者百官則自司徒而下無不在所統矣今乃均列
一職而併數之為六者綱在網中也乾坤之與六子

徒以掌之。司徒曰地官卿，既掌國之敎化，則夫五典出於天，得以敷其敎於民；兆民處於下，使之順其化於上。敎化莫先於禮樂，故立宗伯以掌之。宗伯曰春官卿，既掌國之典禮，則夫天神、地祇、人鬼之事，當治之以直清；上下、尊卑、等列之分，當和之以秩序。敎化、禮樂既以興行，豈無弗率訓典者哉？大者加以甲兵，故邦政掌以司馬。司馬非夏官卿乎？由是六師有統，詰戒兵而奮武烈者，無擾也；邦國用平，强凌弱而衆暴寡者，有警也。小者施以刑罰，故邦禁掌以司宼。司宼非秋官卿乎？於是姦慝隱而難知者，窮詰以求其情；暴亂顯而易見者，刑戮以正其罪。姦慝、暴亂既去，民不可以不奠，故立司空於後，以主國之空土。司空曰冬官卿，士、農、工、賈之雜處，俾有以遂其安居；作、訛、成、易之屢遷，俾有以興其地利。六卿於是乎備，萬事於是乎舉，成周建官之制，孰有要於此哉？

translation_en:
…the Minister of Education (Situ) to take charge of it. The Minister of Education is called the Minister of the Office of Earth (Diguan qing). Since he takes charge of the state's moral instruction and transformation, the Five Constant Relationships that issue from Heaven can thereby be spread as teachings among the people, and the millions of commoners dwelling below are made to conform to the transforming influence from above. In moral instruction and transformation, nothing takes precedence over rites and music; therefore, he established the Minister of Rites (Zongbo) to take charge of them. The Minister of Rites is called the Minister of the Office of Spring (Chunguan qing). Since he takes charge of the state's canonical rites, the affairs of heavenly spirits, earthly deities, and human ghosts ought to be regulated with uprightness and purity, and the distinctions of superior and inferior, noble and base, and graded ranks ought to be harmonized through orderly sequence. Once moral instruction, transformation, rites, and music have been promoted and put into practice, how could there be none who fail to follow the instructive canons? To the major offenders, armor and weapons are applied; therefore, the military administration of the state is placed in the charge of the Minister of War (Sima). Is not the Minister of War the Minister of the Office of Summer (Xiaguan qing)? Through this, the Six Armies have unified command, and in disciplining military forces and displaying martial valor, there is no turmoil; the states and domains are thereby pacified, and the strong who bully the weak and the many who tyrannize the few are given warning. To the minor offenders, punishments and penalties are meted out; therefore, the prohibitions of the state are placed in the charge of the Minister of Justice (Sikou). Is not the Minister of Justice the Minister of the Office of Autumn (Qiuguan qing)? Thereupon, those whose wickednesses are hidden and difficult to know are thoroughly interrogated to discover the true circumstances; those whose violent disorders are manifest and easy to see are punished and executed to rectify their crimes. Once wickedness and violent disorder have been removed, the people cannot but be settled in their dwellings; therefore, he established the Minister of Works (Sikong) last, to preside over the unoccupied lands of the state. The Minister of Works is called the Minister of the Office of Winter (Dongguan qing). Where scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants dwell intermingled, he causes them to have the means to achieve secure habitation; as the agricultural labours of spring sprouting, summer transformation, autumn harvesting, and winter storing repeatedly shift with the seasons, he causes them to have the means to develop the benefits of the land. With this, the Six Ministers are complete, and with this, the myriad affairs are set in motion. In the system of establishing offices in accomplished Zhou, what could be more essential than this?

Yet if we consider the matter further: what the Grand宰 (Zhongzai, Prime Minister) takes charge of is the governance of the state, so from instruction and rites on down, there is nothing not within his charge; what the Prime Minister commands is the hundred officials, so from the Minister of Education on down, there is no one not under his command. That he is now ranked equally in a single office and counted together with the others to make six is because the headrope is within the net. Just as Qian and Kun along with the six sons…

王者重歎以戒農官，既舉天時以勉農事之當勤，復即地利以示豐年之可必。夫務農之道，惟在於及時力田而已。茍能因其時而盡其力，則豐年之慶，豈有不可必者乎？王者之於農官，而發歎以戒之，其重農之意至矣。甞論夫天下之利莫大於農，而天下之勞亦莫過於農也。周之王者其知乎此，故其戒夫農官，
translation_en:
…are arrayed side by side in the eight directions; the six [functions] of the Grand Preceptor (Zhongzai) are arrayed side by side with the five Ministers [sic, 郷 for 卿] among the six offices. Moreover, the Six Ministers divided their duties, each leading his subordinates to guide the Pastors of the Nine Provinces and bring abundance and maturity to the millions of the common people. How could the supreme harmony of the flourishing Zhou have come about without cause?

Book of Odes (Shi)
"Ah, ah, Associate Officials of Agriculture! It is now the end of spring; what more do you seek? How is it with the second-year and third-year fields? Oh, splendid are the wheat and barley; we are about to receive their bright bounty. The bright and glorious Lord on High will bring us a prosperous year." (Ode 276, "Chen gong")
By Zhao Xiang.
Comment by Associate Examiner Admonisher (Yude) Li: The wording and meaning are gentle, subtle, and tactful, sufficient to convey admonition. Reading it, one can still envision the spirit of that age; it may truly be said to have grasped the purport of the Odes.
Comment by Examiner Academician (Xueshi) Chen: It recounts the intention of admonishing the agricultural officials in an intimate and fitting manner.
Comment by Examiner Vice Supervisor of the Household (Shao zhanshi) Wang: The reasoning is clear and the diction fluent, capturing the meaning of the admonition given at that time.

The true king sighed deeply to admonish the agricultural officials: having cited the seasons of Heaven to urge that farming tasks ought to be pursued with diligence, he then pointed to the advantages of the earth to show that a bountiful year could be counted upon with certainty. Now, the way of devoting oneself to agriculture lies solely in working the fields strenuously at the proper time. If one can follow the seasons and exhaust one's strength, how could the blessing of a bountiful year not be assured? That the true king uttered sighs to admonish the agricultural officials shows that his concern for attaching importance to agriculture was supreme. Let us consider that among the benefits of the world none is greater than agriculture, and among the toils of the world none exceeds agriculture. title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
發諸聲嗟形諸氣歎若曰尔保介為農官之副職之
所掌者惟農而已而不攝以他政焉今吾以天道觀
之則斗柄已建辰矣以時令考之則夏正之三月矣
於此而不勉其事焉吾恐時不為人而留也尔之所
當求者今如何哉二歲之田曰新治之為難必也載
芟載柞而其耕澤澤可也田之三歲曰畬用力稍易
必也徂隰徂畛而俶載南畝可也尔無以效之未見
而懈於用力也獨不觀夫麥乎小麥曰來今已實堅
而實好矣大麥曰牟茲又實穎而實栗矣於是申之
===
以於皇于以歎其美利為有成也繼之以厥明于以
見其明賜為可受也夫麥乃先五穀而熟而一歲之
豐凶可以豫占今焉將熟既有以受上帝之明賜矣
則此明昭之上帝又將賜我新畬以豐年焉殆見生
我百穀而收成之多可必也介我稷黍而儲積之厚
可期也其示之以此者實所以深勉之也抑是詩王
者戒農官而作也觀其上文有曰嗟嗟臣工敬尔在
公王釐尔成来咨来茹既總戒羣臣於前矣下文有
曰命我衆人庤乃錢鎛奄觀銍艾蓋又忽見其收成也

以於皇乎以歎其美利為有成也繼之以歎明乎以
見其明賜為可受也夫麥乃先五穀而熟而一歲之
豐凶可以豫占今焉將熟既有以受上帝之明賜矣
則此明昭之上帝又將賜我新畬以豐年焉殆見生
我百穀而收成之多可必也介我稷黍而儲積之厚
可期也其示之以此者實所以深勉之也抑是詩王
者戒農官而作也觀其上文有曰嗟嗟臣工敬爾在
公王釐爾成來咨來茹既總戒羣臣於前矣下文有
曰命我衆人庤乃錢鎛奄觀銍艾蓋又忽見其收成也
punctuated:
發諸聲嗟，形諸氣歎，若曰：「尔保介，為農官之副，職之所掌者惟農而已，而不攝以他政焉。今吾以天道觀之，則斗柄已建辰矣；以時令考之，則夏正之三月矣。於此而不勉其事焉，吾恐時不為人而留也。尔之所當求者，今如何哉？二歲之田曰新，治之為難，必也載芟載柞，而其耕澤澤可也。田之三歲曰畬，用力稍易，必也徂隰徂畛，而俶載南畝可也。尔無以效之未見而懈於用力也。獨不觀夫麥乎？小麥曰來，今已實堅而實好矣；大麥曰牟，茲又實穎而實栗矣。」於是申之以「於皇」，于以歎其美利為有成也；繼之以「厥明」，于以見其明賜為可受也。夫麥乃先五穀而熟，而一歲之豐凶可以豫占。今焉將熟，既有以受上帝之明賜矣，則此明昭之上帝又將賜我新畬以豐年焉。殆見生我百穀，而收成之多可必也；介我稷黍，而儲積之厚可期也。其示之以此者，實所以深勉之也。
抑是詩，王者戒農官而作也。觀其上文有曰：「嗟嗟臣工，敬尔在公。王釐尔成，来咨来茹。」既總戒羣臣於前矣。下文有曰：「命我衆人，庤乃錢鎛，奄觀銍艾。」蓋又忽見其收成也。
translation_en:
…giving voice to his concern in exclamations and expressing it through sighs, as though saying: “You, the baojie, serve as deputy to the agricultural official. Your office is responsible solely for agriculture, without concurrently administering other affairs. Now, when I observe the course of Heaven, the Dipper’s handle already points to chen; when I consult the seasonal calendar, it is already the third month by the Xia reckoning. If you do not exert yourselves in your duties at this time, I fear that the season will not wait for anyone. How, then, should you now pursue what is required of you? A field in its second year is called xin, ‘newly cultivated.’ Working it is difficult: you must cut away the grass and clear the trees, ploughing until the soil is thoroughly loosened. A field in its third year is called yu, ‘established farmland.’ It requires somewhat less effort, but you must still go to the lowlands and the field boundaries and begin work on the southern fields. Do not slacken your efforts because their results are not yet apparent. Have you not observed the grain? Wheat is called lai: its kernels are already firm and good. Barley is called mou: its ears are now full and its kernels well formed.”
He then reinforces this with “Oh, how splendid!” to praise the fine benefits now coming to fruition, and follows it with “his bright bounty” to show that this manifest gift may be received. Wheat and barley ripen before the other grains, and from them one may foretell whether the year will bring abundance or scarcity. Now that they are about to ripen, there is already the prospect of receiving the Lord on High’s manifest bounty. This radiant Lord on High will therefore also grant our newly cultivated and established fields an abundant year. We may soon see him bring forth our hundred grains, assuring us of a plentiful harvest, and enlarge the yield of our millets, giving us hope of ample stores. By setting this prospect before them, the king is truly urging them to exert themselves all the more.
Moreover, this poem was composed by the king to admonish the agricultural officials. Consider its earlier lines: “Ah, ah, you officers! Be reverent in your public duties. The king has assigned you your tasks; come, consult and deliberate.” He has thus already admonished all his officials together at the outset. Later lines say: “Command our multitude to make ready your spades and hoes; soon we shall see the reaping with sickles.” Here, too, he suddenly envisions their harvest.

===
王者於先代之後不惟喜其留而尤惜其去也夫先
代之後統承先王固王者之所當厚也況以微子之
賢而盡朝廟之禮則周之王者安得不有以厚之乎
此所以愛之而不欲其去也歟是詩也微子來見祖
廟之詩而謂之有客者以其為先代之後時王以客
禮待之而不敢臣也夫以微子而於周為客固王者
之所願見也向也逺處封邦既不可得而見一旦來
朝于廟寧不有以遂其願見之心乎一宿曰宿謂之
宿宿則其來甚近也而周人猶以為幸者豈非以其

王者於先代之後，不惟喜其留，而尤惜其去也。夫先代之後，統承先王，固王者之所當厚也。況以微子之賢，而盡朝廟之禮，則周之王者安得不有以厚之乎？此所以愛之而不欲其去也歟！是詩也，微子來見祖廟之詩。而謂之「有客」者，以其為先代之後，時王以客禮待之而不敢臣也。夫以微子而於周為客，固王者之所願見也。向也逺處封邦，既不可得而見；一旦來朝于廟，寧不有以遂其願見之心乎？一宿曰宿，謂之「宿宿」，則其來甚近也，而周人猶以為幸者，豈非以其
translation_en:
Alas! First saying "Ah, ah!" and a second time saying "Ah, ah!"—how supremely did the true kings of Zhou value agriculture!

"There is a guest who stays a night and stays a night; there is a guest who stays two nights and stays two nights. Give him a tether, to tether his horses."
Zhang Jin 章瑾
Associate Examiner Examining Editor Chen comments: The literary thought is unhurried and poised; the intention of detaining the guest at that time is depicted almost to exhaustion—truly a masterpiece.
Examiner Academician Chen comments: The diction suffices to bring out the meaning of the Classic.
Examiner Vice Supervisor of the Household Wang comments: The essay features repeated and thorough argumentation; the generous and sincere spirit of the House of Zhou can be seen herein.

Toward the descendant of a former dynasty, the true king not only rejoices at his staying, but even more regrets his departing. Now, the descendant of a former dynasty carries on the line of the former kings, and is assuredly someone whom a true king ought to treat generously. How much more so when someone of the worthiness of the Viscount of Wei (Weizi 微子) fulfills all the rites of attending court and visiting the ancestral temple—how then could the true king of Zhou fail to treat him with generosity? Is this not why he cherished him and did not wish him to leave? This ode is a poem about the Viscount of Wei coming to appear in the ancestral temple. That it calls him "a guest" is because, as the descendant of a former dynasty, the reigning king treated him with the ritual due a guest and did not dare treat him as a subject. That someone like the Viscount of Wei should be a guest at Zhou made him assuredly someone whom the true king wished to see. Previously, residing far off in his enfeoffed state, he could not be seen; once he came to pay court in the temple, how could this not fulfill the king's desire to see him? Staying one night is called su; calling it "su su" means that his arrival was very recent, yet the people of Zhou still counted it good fortune—was this not because…

title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
有萋有苴敦琢其旅而喜其来乎再宿曰信謂之信
信則其留亦未久也而周人猶以為榮者豈非以其
在彼無惡在此無斁而樂其留乎且斯人也可親而
不可疎也可留而不可去也今焉棄我而歸不識可
以繼此而得見乎於是繾綣之情動於中而留行之
計形諸外盖馬所以載行而縶所以絆其足也於是
而授之縶以縶其馬焉周人之意以為客之宿誠為
我之幸矣而情則未洽也今欲留之烏得不授之縶
乎授之縶則馬不可以行矣客之信信誠為我之榮
===
矣而禮則未周也今欲留之寧可不縶其馬乎縶其
馬則客不可以去矣夫如是庶有以罄吾相與之情
而極吾相待之禮耳吁喜其留者敬之至惜其去者
愛之深周人之於微子何其忠厚之至歟不特此也
觀之上文有曰有客有客亦白其馬則不惟待之以
客而且不敢變其所尚也下文又曰薄言追之左右
綏之則不惟惜其去而且留之無方也周人待先代
之後可謂有加而無已也播諸樂歌以美盛德而告
成功豈不宜哉噫盛矣

punctuated: 有萋有苴、敦琢其旅而喜其来乎？再宿曰信，謂之信信，則其留亦未久也，而周人猶以為榮者，豈非以其在彼無惡、在此無斁而樂其留乎？且斯人也，可親而不可疎也，可留而不可去也。今焉棄我而歸，不識可以繼此而得見乎？於是繾綣之情動於中，而留行之計形諸外。盖馬所以載行，而縶所以絆其足也，於是而授之縶以縶其馬焉。周人之意，以為客之宿，誠為我之幸矣，而情則未洽也；今欲留之，烏得不授之縶乎？授之縶則馬不可以行矣。客之信信，誠為我之榮矣，而禮則未周也；今欲留之，寧可不縶其馬乎？縶其馬則客不可以去矣。夫如是，庶有以罄吾相與之情，而極吾相待之禮耳。吁！喜其留者，敬之至；惜其去者，愛之深。周人之於微子，何其忠厚之至歟！不特此也，觀之上文有曰：「有客有客，亦白其馬。」則不惟待之以客，而且不敢變其所尚也。下文又曰：「薄言追之，左右綏之。」則不惟惜其去，而且留之無方也。周人待先代之後，可謂有加而無已也。播諸樂歌，以美盛德而告成功，豈不宜哉？噫！盛矣。
translation_en:
…reverent and dignified manner and his finely chosen and polished retinue, and so rejoiced at his arrival? Staying for two nights is called xin; calling it "staying two nights and another two nights" (xinxin) means that his stay was still not long, and yet the people of Zhou regarded it as an honor—was this not because "over there he is never hated, and over here he is never tired of," so that they delighted in his staying? Moreover, such a man should be held close and not kept at a distance; he should be detained and not allowed to leave. If now he leaves us and returns home, who knows whether we shall be able to see him again hereafter? Thereupon, feelings of deep attachment were stirred within, and plans to detain him from departing took form without. For horses are the means to carry a traveler on his journey, and a tether is the means to hobble their feet; therefore they gave out tethers to hobble his horses. The thought of the people of Zhou was that the guest's lodging for a night was truly fortunate for us, yet our feelings of fellowship have not been fully satisfied; wishing now to detain him, how could we not give out tethers? Once tethers are given out, the horses cannot set forth. The guest's staying for repeated nights was truly an honor for us, yet our rites of hospitality have not been completely fulfilled; wishing now to detain him, how could we not tether his horses? Once his horses are tethered, the guest cannot depart. In this way, perhaps we may exhaust our feelings of mutual fellowship and carry to the utmost our rites of hospitality toward him.

Alas! To rejoice at his staying is the perfection of respect; to regret his departure is the depth of affection. How utterly loyal and generous were the people of Zhou toward the Viscount of Wei (Weizi)! And not only this: looking at the preceding passage, which says, "There is a guest, there is a guest, and white too are his horses," we see that they not only treated him as a guest, but also did not dare to alter what his dynasty held in esteem. And the following passage says further, "We go in pursuit of him; on the left and right we comfort and stay him," showing that they not only regretted his departure, but sought to detain him by every possible means. In their treatment of the descendants of the former dynasty, the people of Zhou may truly be said to have added kindness upon kindness without end. To set this to musical song in order to praise illustrious virtue and announce completed achievement to the spirits—is it not fitting indeed? Ah, how glorious!

title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
春秋
鄭伯使其弟語來盟桓十四年齊高子來盟閔二年楚
屈完來盟于師僖四年
秦瑛
同考試官脩撰陳批春秋佳作固多求其醇而
無疵者絕少此卷七篇俱稱而來盟篇
尤超眾作
考試官學士陳批講說詳切
考試官少詹事批有發明有斷制
===
來盟由於前定春秋著諸侯有寵愛之私來盟由於
未前定春秋美大夫得奉使之義此鄭語之來不可
與高子屈完而並稱也鄭語之來何盟乎蓋前定之
盟也厲公即位結魯為援武父之信未幾即同師以
伐宋敗宋之師方旋又同好以會曹會而未嘗盟也
故歸甫踰時而弟語踵來奉詞將命周旋於儒書秉
禮之廷刑牲歃血益敦乎講信脩睦之好則斯盟也
蓋嘗有約言而非語之專盟者矣然將命大夫之事
也厲公欲厚於結魯故不靳於寵弟之來欲篤於愛

來盟由於前定，《春秋》著諸侯有寵愛之私；來盟由於未前定，《春秋》美大夫得奉使之義。此鄭語之來，不可與高子、屈完而並稱也。鄭語之來，何盟乎？蓋前定之盟也。厲公即位，結魯為援。武父之信未幾，即同師以伐宋；敗宋之師方旋，又同好以會曹。會而未嘗盟也，故歸甫踰時，而弟語踵來。奉詞將命，周旋於儒書秉禮之廷；刑牲歃血，益敦乎講信脩睦之好。則斯盟也，蓋嘗有約言，而非語之專盟者矣。然將命，大夫之事也。厲公欲厚於結魯，故不靳於寵弟之來；欲篤於愛

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

"The Earl of Zheng sent his younger brother Yu to come and make a covenant" (Fourteenth year of Duke Huan); "Gaozi of Qi came and made a covenant" (Second year of Duke Min); "Qu Wan of Chu came and made a covenant with the army" (Fourth year of Duke Xi).

Qin Ying 秦瑛

Associate Examiner and Senior Compiler Chen comments: While there are certainly many fine compositions on the Spring and Autumn Annals, those that are pure and flawless are exceedingly rare. All seven essays in this scroll are well-matched, and the essay on "Coming to Make a Covenant" especially surpasses the rest.
Examiner and Academician Chen comments: The exposition is detailed and incisive.
Examiner and Vice Supervisor of the Household comments: Possesses both original insight and decisive judgment.

When coming to make a covenant stems from a prior agreement, the Spring and Autumn Annals exposes the feudal lord's private bias of favoritism; when coming to make a covenant stems from what was not agreed upon beforehand, the Spring and Autumn Annals praises the grand master for grasping the righteous duty of an envoy's mission. Thus the coming of Yu of Zheng cannot be spoken of on the same level as Gaozi and Qu Wan. What sort of covenant was the coming of Yu of Zheng? It was a covenant determined beforehand. Upon ascending the throne, Duke Li allied himself with Lu for support. Not long after the pledge of good faith at Wufu, they joined forces to attack Song; just as the army that defeated Song returned, they met again in amity at Cao. They met, yet they had not made a covenant; therefore, barely a season after returning, his younger brother Yu arrived on his heels. Bearing the ruler's words and carrying out his command, he conducted himself at a court steeped in scholarly texts and adherence to ritual; slaughtering the sacrificial victim and smearing its blood on the lips, he further strengthened the amity of cultivating good faith and harmony. Thus this covenant was one for which there had already been a prior agreement in words, and was not a covenant made on Yu's own authority. Yet carrying out diplomatic missions is the business of a grand master. title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
弟又必使之使魯為重友于之義果如是耶春秋於
其来特稱使而書弟書名非所謂来盟由於前定春
秋著諸侯有寵愛之私乎若夫高子屈完之来又何
盟乎盖未前定之盟也天禍魯國慶父構難方殷季
子得政日淺齊使高傒將南陽之甲以覘魯之虛實
桓公伐楚始奇兵以侵蔡遂正兵以擣陘楚使屈完
如中國之師以觀兵之眾寡方二子奉命而来齊楚
之君非有靖難服義一定之言也高子既至惟定僖
公之位而不以兼國廣地為心屈完既来惟照包茅
===
之貢而欣然於徼與同好之歡盟出於已而無專制
之嫌事適其宜而合出疆之義春秋於其来不稱使
而高傒書子屈完書名氏又非所謂来盟由於未前
定春秋予大夫得奉使之義乎抑又論之鄭昭之禍
以群弟之多寵也厲公不鑑其失又使語交政於隣
國則無惑乎異日甯母之盟子華謂子人氏之實違

可動而不能建定難之策後乎屈完晉文城濮之役

translation_en:
…younger brother, he necessarily sent him on the mission to Lu. Was this truly how to honor the duty of fraternal affection? Upon his arrival, the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) specifically states "sent as envoy" and records "younger brother" as well as his personal name—is this not what is meant by "when coming to make a covenant was predetermined, the Spring and Autumn Annals exposes the regional rulers' private partiality in bestowing favor"?

As for the arrival of Master Gao (Gaozi 高子) and Qu Wan 屈完, what sort of covenants were those? They were covenants that had not been predetermined. When Heaven sent disaster upon the state of Lu, the turmoil stirred up by Qingfu 慶父 was at its height, and Jizi 季子 had held the reins of government for only a short time; Qi sent Gao Xi 高傒 to lead the armor of Nanyang 南陽 to spy out Lu's strengths and weaknesses. When Duke Huan 桓公 attacked Chu, he first used a surprise force to invade Cai 蔡 and then advanced with his main army to strike Xing 陘; Chu sent Qu Wan to go to the armies of the Central States to observe the size of their forces. Just when these two men received their commands and came, the rulers of Qi and Chu did not have fixed instructions to pacify the turmoil or submit to righteousness. Once Master Gao arrived, he solely established Duke Xi 僖公 on the throne and did not set his mind on annexing the state or expanding territory; once Qu Wan arrived, he solely attended to the tribute of wrapped rush-grass [?] and gladly sought the joy of mutual amity. The covenants originated from themselves, yet without the suspicion of acting arbitrarily; their actions suited what was appropriate and conformed to the righteous duty of an envoy once beyond his state's borders. Upon their arrival, the Spring and Autumn Annals does not state "sent as envoy," while for Gao Xi it records the title "Master" (zi 子) and for Qu Wan it records his personal name and clan name—is this not in turn what is meant by "when coming to make a covenant was not predetermined, the Spring and Autumn Annals commends Great Officers for grasping the righteous duty of serving as envoys"?

Furthermore, let us discuss it: the calamity of Duke Zhao of Zheng 鄭昭 arose because his younger brothers enjoyed excessive favor. Duke Li 厲公 did not take warning from that failure and again sent Yu 語 to engage in state affairs with neighboring countries; thus it is no wonder that on a later day, at the covenant of Ningmu 甯母, Zihua 子華 said that the Ziren 子人氏 clan actually defied their ruler's commands. Prior to Master Gao, when Zhongsun Qiu 仲孫湫 came, he merely knew that Lu upheld the rites of Zhou and could not yet be shaken, but he was unable to establish a plan for settling the turmoil; subsequent to Qu Wan, at Duke Wen of Jin's 晉文 battle of Chengpu 城濮, the Viscount of Chu 楚子 did not wish to fight, yet Ziyu 子玉 forced it, thereby bringing about the rout of the Chu army. The feudal lords made a covenant at Kuiqiu." title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
於盟洮焉安王室於有事之時尊王人於諸侯之上
由是列侯邦君咸重乎桓公之義而逃盟之鄭遂悔
其從楚之非奔走於兵車之會乞盟乎壇坫之間嚮
也棄義而逃今也慕義而至則伯功之著足以感夫
人也為何如哉明年宰孔致胙葵丘有會赫然加勞
賜級之命懔然下拜登受之恭迨夫宰孔既歸而葵
丘有盟示以一王之禁敦以言歸之好桓之伯業至
是為極盛矣夫何震矜一萌無以堅安攘之志西則
否矣遂為宰孔之所窺由是舉動頓殊而外患輒起
===
馴至淮夷病鄫九國之師同會于淮以謀之諸侯咸
在而人心已不協役人夜呼而城鄫之不果則伯業
之終無以恤乎人也又何如哉吁即鄭伯之乞盟于
以見桓公信義之著在於盟洮之日即會淮之無功
又以見桓公驕矜之心萌於葵丘之盛比事以觀伯
者之功過昭昭矣雖然桓伯之盛衰不特此也于洮

punctuated: 於盟洮焉。安王室於有事之時，尊王人於諸侯之上。由是列侯邦君，咸重乎桓公之義，而逃盟之鄭，遂悔其從楚之非，奔走於兵車之會，乞盟乎壇坫之間。嚮也棄義而逃，今也慕義而至，則伯功之著，足以感夫人也為何如哉！明年宰孔致胙，葵丘有會，赫然加勞賜級之命，懔然下拜登受之恭。迨夫宰孔既歸，而葵丘有盟，示以一王之禁，敦以言歸之好，桓之伯業，至是為極盛矣。夫何震矜一萌，無以堅安攘之志，「西則否矣」，遂為宰孔之所窺。由是舉動頓殊，而外患輒起，馴至淮夷病鄫，九國之師同會于淮以謀之。諸侯咸在，而人心已不協；役人夜呼，而城鄫之不果。則伯業之終無以恤乎人也又何如哉！吁！即鄭伯之乞盟，于以見桓公信義之著，在於盟洮之日；即會淮之無功，又以見桓公驕矜之心，萌於葵丘之盛。比事以觀，伯者之功過昭昭矣。雖然，桓伯之盛衰，不特此也。于洮以前，二幽盟而同尊之義明，召陵盟而帖荆之績著，首止之定王儲，寗毋之通王貢，何莫非伯業之盛也！葵丘以後，于鹹會而違專封之禁，牡丘會而緩救徐…
translation_en:
…at the covenant of Tao. He stabilized the royal house in its time of trouble and honored the King's envoy above the feudal lords. Consequently, the assembled lords and rulers of states all esteemed the righteousness of Duke Huan, and Zheng, which had previously fled the covenant, regretted the wrongness of its having followed Chu. It hastened to the assembly of war chariots and begged for a covenant among the altar mounds. Earlier it had abandoned righteousness and fled; now it admired righteousness and came. How great indeed was the manifest achievement of the hegemon in its capacity to move others!

The following year, Zai Kong (the Royal Steward Kong) delivered the sacrificial meat at the assembly of Kuiqiu. Illustrious was the King's charge bestowing rewards for toil and dispensing him from descending the steps; reverent was the Duke's respect in descending to bow and ascending to receive the gift. Once Zai Kong had returned home, there was the covenant at Kuiqiu, which proclaimed the prohibitions of the one King and strengthened the amity of returning together in peace. Huan's hegemonic enterprise reached its utmost flourishing at this point.

Yet how was it that once arrogance and boastfulness sprouted, he had no means to hold firm his resolve to pacify the realm and repel the tribes, and—that "as for advancing westward, he will not do so"—was thus seen through by Zai Kong? From this point on, his conduct suddenly changed and external troubles repeatedly arose, leading gradually to the Huai Yi harassing Zeng, whereupon the armies of nine states met together at the Huai River to take counsel on it. The feudal lords were all present, yet men's hearts were already out of harmony; the laborers cried out in the night, and the walling of Zeng came to nothing. What then are we to say of his hegemonic enterprise ending without the means to succor others!

Alas! From the Earl of Zheng's begging for a covenant, one can see that the manifestation of Duke Huan's trustworthiness and righteousness lay in the day of the covenant at Tao; from the lack of success at the assembly of the Huai, one can also see that Duke Huan's heart of pride and boastfulness sprouted at the height of Kuiqiu. When we set these events side by side to observe them, the merits and faults of the hegemon are clear indeed.

Even so, the rise and decline of Huan's hegemony were not limited to these instances alone. Before the meeting at Tao: the two covenants at You made clear the duty of jointly honoring the King; the covenant at Shaoling made manifest the achievement of subduing Jing (Chu); the settling of the royal heir at Shouzhi; and the opening of the flow of royal tribute at Ningmu—which of these was not the flourishing of his hegemonic enterprise? title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
其就賢而體遠孰若從事於大學是故賢者有德之
士也我能就之則賢者固好我而示我以周行矣遠
者疏遠之臣也我能體之則遠者固親我而乃心王
室矣賢而謂之就則必以貴下賤而重其禮也可知
遠而謂之體則設以身處其地而察其心也可見就
賢也體遠也若可以化乎民矣然但能聳動其觀聽
而未足以洽於心振起其一時而未足以及於遠君
子必欲化民成俗如唐虞之於變時雍成周之化行江
漢者夫豈在他求哉惟在務學以盡乎明德新民之
===
功而已必也格物致知以窮其理誠意正心以脩其
身時教之有正業者于以藏焉而脩焉退息必有居學
者于以息焉而游焉如是則衆物之表裏精粗無不
到而吾心之全體大用無不明矣由是推之以化民
成俗則民無不化俗無不成夫豈足以動衆者之比
哉愚故曰親賢類而感乎人者不足以洽民導民心
而化於善者必本於為學者此也抑考學記一篇言
君子之學不一而足以見先王之為治不在乎他而
必本於學也觀之此章尤為有序始曰發慮憲求善

translation_en: …rather than approaching the worthy and empathizing with the distant, how much better to devote oneself to the Great Learning? Therefore, the worthy are men of virtue; if I can approach them, the worthy will surely be fond of me and show me the grand highway of the Way. The distant are ministers who are far removed; if I can empathize with them, the distant will surely feel close to me and set their hearts upon the royal house. As for the worthy, when it is called "approaching" them, one knows that it surely means humbling the noble before the lowly and giving weight to ritual courtesy for them; as for the distant, when it is called "empathizing" with them, one sees that it means putting oneself in their place and examining their hearts. Approaching the worthy and empathizing with the distant would seem sufficient to transform the people; yet they can only stir what people see and hear, and are not enough to permeate their hearts; they can rouse people for a single moment, and are not enough to reach afar. If the gentleman is determined to transform the people and perfect customs—so that they become like the transformation and harmonious concord of the eras of Tang Yao and Yu Shun, or the moral transformation spreading to the Jiang and Han rivers under flourishing Zhou—how could this be sought in anything else? It lies solely in devoting oneself to learning so as to fulfill the work of illuminating luminous virtue and renewing the people. One must investigate things and extend knowledge in order to exhaust their principles, and make the intentions sincere and rectify the mind in order to cultivate one's person. In the regular studies of seasonal instruction, one stores up and cultivates them in mind; in the residential studies required during periods of retirement and rest, one rests and strolls at ease in them. When it is like this, then the exterior and interior, the subtle and coarse of all things will be thoroughly reached, and the entire substance and great functioning of one's mind will be completely illuminated. Extending this to transform the people and perfect customs, there will be no people untransformed and no customs unperfected—how could that which merely suffices to move the multitude be compared to this? Therefore I say: drawing close to the category of the worthy and moving others is not enough to permeate the people; guiding the people's hearts and transforming them toward goodness must be rooted in engaging in learning—this is what is meant. Moreover, if we examine the "Record on the Subject of Education" (Xueji) as a whole, it speaks of the gentleman's learning in more ways than one, showing that the governance of the former kings did not lie in anything else, but was necessarily rooted in learning. Looking at this passage, its sequence is especially orderly. First it says: "Sending forth thoughts regulated by laws and seeking the good…

… [seeking good from] the multitude is sufficient to secure a modest reputation [?], yet insufficient to move the multitude"; here it says: "Approaching the worthy and showing consideration for the distant is sufficient to move the multitude, yet insufficient to transform the people"; and it further says: "If a gentleman wishes to transform the people and perfect customs, must it not be through learning!" Its practice is weightier at each successive stage, and its efficacy is deeper at each successive stage; those of later times who rule over men ought to ponder upon this.

"Therefore, when the gentleman wears his robes, he adorns them with the demeanor of a gentleman; having that demeanor, he adorns it with the speech of a gentleman; bringing that speech to completion, he substantiates it with the virtue of a gentleman."
By Wei Guan 韋觀.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Senior Compiler Ma: What this topic emphasizes lies in "substantiating it with virtue." Most compositions discuss it on an equal footing with robes, demeanor, and speech, quite failing to understand what is secondary and what is primary. This essay alone is able to grasp the meaning clearly, and its prose flows smoothly; the author must be well-versed in the Classic of Rites (Lijing).
Comment by Examiner and Academician Chen: Plain and substantial, yet possessing literary grace; worthy of note.
Comment by Examiner and Vice Director of the Household Administration Wang: This composition places the ultimate emphasis on virtue, which is enough to show that he has a clear understanding of the teaching.

When a gentleman presides over the people, he not only desires that the refinement adorning him on the outside be completely provided in every respect, but even more desires that the fundamental substance within him be completely fulfilled in every respect. Now, the Way of the gentleman prizes the mutual correspondence of the inner and the outer. If he merely has refinement adorning him on the outside, while lacking the fundamental substance within, how could he be worthy to occupy a position above and preside over those below? Now then, the ritual robes prescribed by the former kings are the robes of the gentleman; being grave, reverent, and dignified is the demeanor of the gentleman; what is rooted in the mind and issues forth from the mouth …

text:
者謂之言得於己而見諸行者謂之德服其服固有
儀於外矣然不文之以容則無以稱其服文以容固
可稱其服矣然不文之以辭則無以稱其容故不徒
服君子之服而又飾以君子之容然後有威之可
畏有儀之可象也不惟飾以君子之容而又文以
君子之辭然後有言之可法有訓之可從也辭既遂
矣外既飾矣尤不可以不實其內必使和順之實蘊
於中者純然粹然而無一德之或虧仁聖之理蓄於
己者盎然睟然而無一理之或歉萃乎萬理之咸備
===
溢乎四體之充周君子之德既有諸己然後衣服容
貌之飾於躬者為有德之儀言語辭氣之發於口者
為有德之辭容貌辭氣皆德之符而非徒然者矣豈
非文之飾於外者無不備本之實於內者無不充乎
抑考魯論有曰知及之仁能守之不莊以涖之則民
不敬亦臨民之道也但彼則先德行而後威儀此則
先威儀而後德行何也蓋魯論之言由己以及人明
德而後新民也表記之言由表而達裏泝流而窮其
源也雖有不同而其貴乎有德則一而已吁旨哉

punctuated: 者，謂之言；得於己而見諸行者，謂之德。服其服，固有儀於外矣，然不文之以容，則無以稱其服；文以容，固可稱其服矣，然不文之以辭，則無以稱其容。故不徒服君子之服，而又飾以君子之容，然後有威之可畏、有儀之可象也；不惟飾以君子之容，而又文以君子之辭，然後有言之可法、有訓之可從也。辭既遂矣，外既飾矣，尤不可以不實其內。必使和順之實蘊於中者，純然粹然而無一德之或虧；仁聖之理蓄於己者，盎然睟然而無一理之或歉。萃乎萬理之咸備，溢乎四體之充周。君子之德既有諸己，然後衣服容貌之飾於躬者，為有德之儀；言語辭氣之發於口者，為有德之辭。容貌辭氣，皆德之符，而非徒然者矣。豈非文之飾於外者無不備，本之實於內者無不充乎？抑考《魯論》有曰：「知及之，仁能守之，不莊以涖之，則民不敬。」亦臨民之道也。但彼則先德行而後威儀，此則先威儀而後德行，何也？蓋《魯論》之言，由己以及人，明德而後新民也；《表記》之言，由表而達裏，泝流而窮其源也。雖有不同，而其貴乎有德，則一而已。吁！旨哉！
translation_en:
… [that which stems from the mind and issues from the mouth] is called speech; that which is attained within oneself and manifested in action is called virtue. Wearing such garments certainly provides external deportment, yet if one does not refine it with countenance and bearing, there is no way to match those garments. Refining it with countenance and bearing can certainly match the garments, yet if one does not refine it with speech, there is no way to match that countenance and bearing. Therefore, one does not merely wear the garments of a gentleman, but also adorns them with the countenance and bearing of a gentleman; only then is there majesty to be revered and deportment to be emulated. One not only adorns oneself with the countenance and bearing of a gentleman, but also refines them with the speech of a gentleman; only then are there words to serve as a model and teachings to be followed. Once one's speech is accomplished and the exterior is adorned, it is all the more imperative not to leave the interior unsubstantiated. One must ensure that the substance of harmony and compliance treasured within is pure and unadulterated, without a single virtue lacking; and that the principles of benevolence and sageliness accumulated in oneself are abundant and lustrous, without a single principle deficient—gathering all the myriad principles in complete readiness, overflowing to fill the four limbs. Once the virtue of the gentleman is possessed within oneself, only then do the garments and countenance adorning the person become the deportment of one who possesses virtue, and the words and tones issuing from the mouth become the speech of one who possesses virtue. Countenance, bearing, words, and tone are all tallies of virtue, and are not there in vain. Is this not a case of the refinement adorning the exterior being completely prepared, and the root substantiated within being completely full?

Furthermore, if we examine the Analects (Lulun), it says: "When one's knowledge is sufficient to attain it, and one's benevolence is capable of keeping it, if one does not preside over them with gravity, the common people will not be reverent." This too is the way of presiding over the people. Yet that passage puts virtuous conduct first and majestic deportment after, whereas this passage puts majestic deportment first and virtuous conduct after—why is that? It is because the words of the Analects proceed from oneself to extend to others, illuminating bright virtue and only thereafter renewing the people; whereas the words of the "Record on Example" ("Biaoji") proceed from the exterior to reach the interior, tracing the stream back to exhaust its source. Although they differ in approach, in prizing the possession of virtue they are one and the same. Ah, how profound in meaning!
