論曰：天下之方圓，非但規矩也，而皆取法於規矩；天下之人倫，非但聖人也，而皆取法於聖人。蓋規矩為方圓之至，聖人為人倫之至。方圓而不法於規矩，固不可以成器；人倫而不法於聖人，其可以為人乎？且邃古之初，未有聖人也，其世混沌，其民顓蒙。聚處以相尊也，而為君臣；生育以相愛也，而為父子；同出也，而為兄弟；同室也，而為夫婦；至於居以相比、行以相旅，而為朋友。蓋蚩々然而已矣，蠢々然而已矣。於斯時也，

Discourse

"The sage is the perfection of human relationships."
Liu Dingzhi 劉定之

Associate Examiner, Senior Compiler Sun 孫 comments: The conception is lofty and the phrasing is fluent; reading it is delightful.
Examiner, Academician Chen 陳 comments: The language is neither commonplace nor superficial, beyond the reach of his peers.
Examiner, Vice Supervisor of the Household Wang 王 comments: The discourse topic is upright, grand, and straightforward, such that anyone can write on it, yet the multitude of trite clichés is truly contemptible and tiresome. This composition alone manages to transform the stale into the extraordinary; he must be a scholar of true learning.

The discourse states: The squares and circles in the world are not limited to the compass and square alone, yet all take the compass and square as their standard; human relationships in the world are not limited to the sages alone, yet all take the sages as their standard. For the compass and square are the perfection of squares and circles, and the sage is the perfection of human relationships. If squares and circles do not take the compass and square as their standard, they certainly cannot form vessels; if human relationships do not take the sage as their standard, how can one be a human being? Moreover, at the beginning of remote antiquity, there were not yet sages; that world was primordial and undifferentiated, and its people were simple and ignorant. Dwelling together in mutual respect, they became ruler and minister; giving birth and nurturing in mutual affection, they became father and son; born of the same origin, they became elder and younger brothers; sharing the same chamber, they became husband and wife; and as for dwelling as neighbors and traveling as companions, they became friends. 不知所謂人倫之理而况知所謂盡人倫之理
之至者乎雖然不知所謂人倫之理而猶未至
於病夫人倫也迨世俗既降民偽愈滋人倫有
不能盡者於是天生聖人以為之準則焉蓋君
臣之義違而或至於暴慢也而堯之平章協和
為君道之至舜之温恭祗承為臣道之至此天
下之君臣所以於此取法也父子之親乖而或
至於頑嚚也而文王丕顯之謨為父道之至武
王丕承之烈為子道之至此天下之父子所以
===

之雝々在宫者為至豈不於此取法乎河漘之
葛兄弟之恩疎矣而聖人之常棣相友為至又
不於此取法乎至於久要而忘其信久交而怠
其敬朋友之道失矣而聖人之與國人交而止
於信者又無不至亦惡得而不取法乎孟軻氏
之為此言而舉唐虞聖人之事以見其餘美哉

translation_en: … they did not know what is called the principle of human relationships, and still less did they know what is called the ultimate perfection of fulfilling the principle of human relationships! Even so, though they did not know what is called the principle of human relationships, they had not yet reached the point of doing harm to human relationships. When the customs of the world declined and deceit among the people grew ever more rampant, there were those who could not fulfill their human relationships, and thereupon Heaven gave birth to the sages to serve as standards for them. For when righteousness between ruler and minister was violated, sometimes reaching the point of tyranny and arrogance, Yao’s distinguishing the able and harmonizing the myriad states served as the ultimate perfection of the way of the ruler, and Shun’s gentle reverence and respectful compliance served as the ultimate perfection of the way of the minister; this is why rulers and ministers throughout the world take their model here. When affection between father and son went awry, sometimes reaching the point of obstinacy and insincerity, King Wen’s illustriously manifest plans served as the ultimate perfection of the way of the father, and King Wu’s grandly inherited achievements served as the ultimate perfection of the way of the son; this is why fathers and sons throughout the world take their model here. As seen in the ode of the motherwort in the valley, propriety between husband and wife had grown thin, yet the sage’s being harmonious in the palace served as the ultimate perfection—how could one not take one’s model here? As seen in the ode of the kudzu on the riverbanks, kindness between brothers had grown distant, yet the sage’s fraternal affection as in the cherry-apple ode served as the ultimate perfection—again, how could one not take one’s model here? And when old promises are forgotten in their trustworthiness and long-standing associations slacken in their respect, the way of friends is lost; yet the sage’s resting in trustworthiness in his intercourse with the people of the state is also in every way the ultimate perfection—so how could one fail to take one’s model there as well? In making this statement, Meng Ke (Mencius) cited the deeds of the sages of Tang and Yu (Yao and Shun) to illustrate the rest—how admirable was his concern for the moral instruction of the world! Even so, in the age of high antiquity, before there were sages to serve as models, the principles of human relationships each resided within people’s own persons, and none failed to follow the natural…

Associate Examiner Examining Editor Chen comments: This composition answers each point of the question in turn; both its diction and its reasoning are superior. The following four essays are likewise, and the first two sessions were especially fine—surely a scholar of learning.

Where there is a sage ruler of an age, there are surely the institutions and works of that age; where there are the institutions and works of an age, there is accordingly the flourishing governance of that age. For institutions and works have an ancient and a modern, whereas the Way of the sages has neither ancient nor modern. That whereby the former sages handed down teachings for the world was indeed rooted in this Way; and how could that whereby later sages succeeded to Heaven and established the supreme standard lie outside this Way? Humbly reflecting: Grand Progenitor Emperor Gao (Taizu Gaohuangdi 太祖高皇帝), through sage spirituality and civil and martial virtue, opened up great peace for ten thousand generations; Grand Ancestor Emperor Wen (Taizong Wenhuangdi 太宗文皇帝), through divine achievements and sage virtue, inherited the great enterprise of unified rule. title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
發其善心懲創其逸志雖唐虞三代之典謨訓
誥古者聖賢之嘉言善行豈復有過於此者乎
盖嘗求之道之大原出於天具於人心而為善
不以知而加多不以愚而加損人所固有之理
不待求之於外但人拘於氣稟汨於物欲是以
全其善者寡矣而為之者不過復其本然者耳
豈待為之而後有哉若夫善施於人不求知不
責報故謂之陰隲是故惻隱之心人皆有之吾
能推之則非仁不為矣羞惡之心人皆有之吾
===
能推之則非義不取矣為善之實孰大於此天
人一理通達無間人之善既積於己天之報必
應乎人感應之機捷於桴鼓其與易之積善餘
慶書之惠迪則吉之旨異世而同符也古之人
為善者孰過舜與顏子觀夫取諸人以為善得
一善而服膺雖有自然勉强之殊而其孳孳拳
拳則一顏子以舜自期則曰舜何人也予何人
也有為者亦若是後之人以顏子自期則曰顏
何人哉希之則是於乎士希賢而為善者必法

人一理通達無間人之善既積於已天之報必
應乎人感應之機捷於桴鼓其與易之積善餘
慶書之恵迪則吉之旨異世而同符也古之人
為善者孰過舜與顏子觀夫取諸人以為善得
一善而服膺雖有自然勉强之殊而其孳孳拳
拳則一顏子以舜自期則曰舜何人也予何人
也有為者亦若是後之人以顏子自期則曰顏
何人哉希之則是於乎士希賢而為善者必法
punctuated: 發其善心，懲創其逸志，雖唐、虞、三代之典、謨、訓、誥，古者聖賢之嘉言善行，豈復有過於此者乎？蓋嘗求之，道之大原出於天，具於人心，而為善，不以知而加多，不以愚而加損，人所固有之理，不待求之於外。但人拘於氣稟，汨於物欲，是以全其善者寡矣，而為之者不過復其本然者耳，豈待為之而後有哉？若夫善施於人，不求知，不責報，故謂之陰隲。是故惻隱之心，人皆有之，吾能推之，則非仁不為矣；羞惡之心，人皆有之，吾能推之，則非義不取矣。為善之實，孰大於此？天人一理，通達無間。人之善既積於己，天之報必應乎人，感應之機，捷於桴鼓，其與《易》之「積善餘慶」、《書》之「惠迪則吉」之旨，異世而同符也。古之人為善者，孰過舜與顏子？觀夫取諸人以為善，得一善而服膺，雖有自然、勉强之殊，而其孳孳拳拳則一。顏子以舜自期，則曰：「舜何人也？予何人也？有為者亦若是。」後之人以顏子自期，則曰：「顏何人哉？希之則是。」於乎！士希賢而為善者，必法
translation_en:
…inspire their good hearts and chasten their wayward inclinations. Even the canons, counsels, instructions, and announcements of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties, or the admirable words and good deeds of the ancient sages and worthies—how could they surpass these?

If we seek into the matter, the great origin of the Way comes forth from Heaven, is endowed in the human mind, and constitutes goodness. It is neither increased by wisdom nor diminished by folly; as the principle inherently possessed by human beings, it does not wait to be sought from outside. Yet people are constrained by their physical endowment and submerged in material desires, and therefore those who keep their goodness whole are few. Those who practice goodness are merely restoring their original nature—how could goodness exist only after one practices it? As for bestowing goodness upon others without seeking recognition or demanding recompense, that is why it is called "unseen reward" (yinzhi). Therefore, all people have the mind of commiseration; if I can extend it, I will do nothing that is not humane. All people have the mind of shame and dislike; if I can extend it, I will take nothing that is not righteous. As for the substance of doing good, what could be greater than this?

Heaven and humanity share a single principle, communicating without barrier. Once a person's goodness is accumulated within oneself, Heaven's recompense will surely respond to that person; the mechanism of stimulus and response is swifter than the drumstick to the drum. This tallies across different ages with the meaning of "accumulating goodness brings superabundant blessings" in the Book of Changes (Yi) and "following the right path brings good fortune" in the Book of Documents (Shu).

Among the ancients who practiced goodness, who surpassed Shun and Master Yan (Yanzi)? Observe how the one took from others in order to do good, while the other obtained a single good thing and clasped it firmly to his breast: although there was a difference between effortless spontaneity and strenuous effort, their tireless diligence and earnest devotion were one and the same. Master Yan took Shun as his own standard and said, "What sort of man was Shun? What sort of man am I? Anyone who makes the effort can also be like this." People of later times took Master Yan as their own standard and said, "What sort of man was Yan? To aspire to be like him is to be like him." Alas! A scholar who aspires to become a worthy and practices goodness must model himself…

兩儀未判，道在太極；兩儀既分，道在聖人。太極者，道之體也；聖人者，體斯道者也。堯、舜以是道傳之禹、湯，禹、湯以是道傳之文、武、周公，其道固無異也。粤稽孟軻氏有曰：「堯、舜之道，孝弟而已矣。」盖孝弟者，仁義之始也，能自孝弟之道以行
translation_en:
… Yanzi (顏子), and a worthy who aspires to be a sage in doing good must model himself on the Great Shun (大舜). Therefore, the Great Shun received the abdication of the throne and was certain to obtain emolument, rank, fame, and longevity; Yanzi heard the Way and was enshrined as a correlate in the temple sacrifices to Confucius (孔子). The Great Shun obtained blessings in his own time, and Yanzi obtained blessings for ten thousand generations—who could say that this was not rooted in doing good?

The imperial compositions have been brilliantly promulgated, and officials and commoners obey and submit to them; all know to encourage good and punish evil, and none fail to be transformed and become harmonious. How fortunate are this age and this people! I, a foolish student, have cherished these teachings in my heart for years; now, having received this perceptive question, I set forth the general outline in reply.

Before the Two Modes [Heaven and Earth] were separated, the Way resided in the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji 太極); once the Two Modes were divided, the Way resided in the sages. The Supreme Ultimate is the substance of the Way; the sages are those who embody this Way. Yao (堯) and Shun (舜) transmitted this Way to Yu (禹) and Tang (湯), and Yu and Tang transmitted this Way to King Wen (文王), King Wu (武王), and the Duke of Zhou (周公); their Way was assuredly no different. Examining the words of Mencius (Meng Ke 孟軻), he said: "The Way of Yao and Shun is simply filial piety and fraternal respect." For filial piety and fraternal respect are the beginning of benevolence and righteousness; if one is able to proceed from the Way of filial piety and fraternal respect to practice…

text:
仁義無往而不得矣又曰禹惡旨酒而好善言
湯執中立賢無方文王視民如傷望道而未之
見武王不泄邇不忘遠盖堯舜之孝弟行仁義
之道於家者也禹惡旨酒而好善言脩仁義之
行於身而取仁義之善於人者也湯之所以執
中者用仁義之道也所以立賢者圖仁義之治
也文王視民如傷推仁義之澤於民也望道而
未之見全仁義之道於巳也武王之不泄邇不
忘遠又何往而非任此道於悠久而不息哉數
===
聖人之道固非有二也孟子特各因其一事而
言之耳非謂禹不能執中立賢而湯却泄邇忘
遠也考之他書稱其德又極盛若六經所載固
不暇詳舉先儒亦謂聖人無不盛孟子叙述以
詔萬世何獨舉此盖孝弟者人倫之大而四事

言矣今夫人君一心所存之道孰有外於仁義禮
智四者前乎唐堯虞舜之協和萬邦而尊為天子
者無非行此道也後乎禹湯文武之典常相率
而謨烈相承者無非推此道也是以百姓昭明
而黎民有於變之休民協于中而四方有風動
之美巍々乎其有成功蕩々乎民無能名二帝
之功業無以加也聲教之被訖于四海彰信兆
民式于九圍明慎而萬民和垂拱而天下治三
王之功業不可尚也二帝三王功業之盛
===
何莫非是道之著乎故孔子稱舜無為而治者
以此也夫豈有出於是道之外哉是以後之為
治者莫不以唐虞三代為法舜之無為而治固
不可尚矣幾之以簡靜者則亦有其人焉漢之
文帝躬脩玄默政尚清靜與民休息可謂能簡
靜矣夫治固貴簡靜苟不以道為本則亦黃老
之無為耳何足以言聖人之道是故簡以道為
本則其簡也能御煩矣靜以道為本則其靜也
能制動矣徒能簡者未必不失於疎略徒能靜

Now as for the Way preserved within the single mind of the ruler of men, how could anything lie outside the four principles of benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, and wisdom? In earlier times, Tang Yao and Yu Shun, who harmonized the myriad states and were revered as Sons of Heaven, did nothing other than practice this Way; in later times, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, who led one another in upholding the constant norms and succeeded one another in grand counsels and illustrious achievements, did nothing other than extend this Way. Therefore, the hundred clans were brightly enlightened and the black-haired people enjoyed the blessing of universal transformation; the people were brought into harmony with the mean and the four quarters displayed the beauty of being stirred as by the wind. Lofty were their successes, and vast, so that the people could find no name for them—nothing could be added to the meritorious achievements of the Two Emperors! Their moral prestige and teachings reached to the Four Seas; they manifested trustworthiness to the millions of people and set a model across the Nine Regions; through clear circumspection the myriad people were harmonized, and by letting their robes hang down with folded hands the realm was governed—nothing could surpass the meritorious achievements of the Three Kings! Could the flourishing of the meritorious achievements of the Two Emperors and Three Kings be anything other than the manifestation of this Way? Therefore, when Confucius praised Shun for governing through non-action, it was because of this. How could there be anything outside of this Way? For this reason, those who engaged in governance in later ages all took Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties as their model. Shun's governing through non-action indeed cannot be surpassed, yet as for approaching it through simplicity and tranquility, there was also someone who did so. Emperor Wen of the Han personally cultivated profound silence, esteemed purity and tranquility in governance, and gave rest and recuperation to the people; he may well be called capable of simplicity and tranquility. Now governance certainly values simplicity and tranquility, yet if it does not take the Way as its foundation, it is merely the non-action of Huang-Lao—how could it be sufficient to speak of the Way of the Sages? Therefore, when simplicity takes the Way as its foundation, that simplicity is able to master complexity; when tranquility takes the Way as its foundation, that tranquility is able to control activity. … those who are merely able to be quiet will not necessarily avoid slipping into laxity and negligence. The reason why the governance of Emperor Wen of the Han was only sufficient to make the people prosperous, yet could not bring rites, music, and moral transformation to his own age—was it not because he had not fully realized the Way of the Two Emperors and Three Kings?

If today we wish to pursue simplicity and quietude while causing the Way to prevail throughout the realm, how could there be any other method? It lies solely in practicing the Way of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom. Therefore, in benevolence, nothing is greater than bestowing kindness, yet without wealth one certainly cannot speak of kindness. One must regulate the people's fields and dwellings, lighten their taxes and levies, and benefit them on the basis of what they themselves find beneficial. Once the common people have enough, with whom could the ruler lack sufficiency? Is this not being wealthy without hoarding in treasuries? In righteousness, nothing is greater than the use of arms, yet without awe-inspiring majesty one certainly cannot speak of arms. One must cultivate civil virtue and rouse military defense, securing order while peace already prevails and dissolving calamities before they take form; then one will command awe without going to battle. Propriety values harmony, yet without yielding one certainly cannot achieve harmony. Therefore, one must foster a culture of integrity and a sense of shame above, and block the gates of eager self-advancement below; then will those who are moved by witnessing such example need to wait for exhortation and leadership before they yield? Wisdom values discrimination, yet without clear insight one certainly cannot discriminate. Therefore, one must see clearly with the eyes of the four quarters and hear clearly with the ears of the four quarters, seek the reality behind blame and praise, and mirror the true circumstances of right and wrong; then will what is gained through hearing and seeing need to wait for nitpicking scrutiny before it becomes clear?

When it is like this, the Way will flourish above and governance will be admirable below. There are not two Ways in the world, and antiquity and the present share the same single principle; how could there be anything practicable in antiquity that is not practicable today? I reverently reflect that Your Majesty, with the mind of the Two Emperors and Three Kings, carries out the governance of the Two Emperors and Three Kings. 三代而上，文武無二道；三代而下，文武有二途。文武無二道者，入則百揆，出則徂征，如禹之於唐、虞，「文武吉甫」之於周是也。文武有二途者，文以武為悍，武以文為迂，歴代不可以勝計也。此三代而上所以皆全才，三代而下所以為不能及也歟！今夫武者，所以戡禍亂、除暴虐，雖安而不可棄，雖治而不可忘，誠有國者之大事也。有武者固不可以無文，有文者尤不可以無武，故孔子曰：「有文事者必有武備。」是以春秋之時，論將者尤貴詩、書、禮、樂，論戰者猶貴仁、義、禮、信，盖非文…

From the Three Dynasties on up, civil and military affairs were not two separate ways; from the Three Dynasties on down, civil and military affairs became two distinct paths. Where civil and military were not two separate ways, inside the court one served as General Regulator (Baikui 百揆) and outside the court one went forth on punitive expeditions—such was Yu 禹 under Tang 唐 [Yao 堯] and Yu 虞 [Shun 舜], and "Ji Fu 吉甫, civil and military" under the Zhou 周. Where civil and military became two distinct paths, civil officials regarded military men as fierce brutes, while military men regarded civil officials as pedantic; through successive dynasties, such cases have been too numerous to count. Is this not why from the Three Dynasties on up men were all complete talents, whereas from the Three Dynasties on down men have been unable to match them? Now, military power is the means by which to quell calamity and disorder and to eradicate tyranny and cruelty. Even in times of peace it must not be abandoned, and even in times of good order it must not be forgotten; truly it is a great affair of those who possess a state. Those who possess military capability certainly cannot be without civil culture, and those who possess civil culture even more so cannot be without military capability. Therefore Confucius said: "One who has civil affairs must have military preparations." … there is no way to win the allegiance of the multitude, and without martial prowess there is no way to overawe the enemy. Employing the civil and the martial together is truly the art of enduring stability—how could they be divided into two? Thus, at the Campaign of Bi in the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), the Viscount of Chu remarked: "Martial prowess has seven virtues, and I do not possess a single one of them." The seven virtues are called: suppressing violence, gathering in weapons, preserving the great, establishing merit, giving peace to the people, harmonizing the multitude, and enriching wealth. Viewed from this perspective, the utility of martial prowess is great indeed; how could it merely be limited to punitive expeditions and campaigning!

Alas! Weapons are instruments of ill omen, and warfare is a perilous affair. One certainly cannot be without method, yet neither can one be rigidly bound by method. During the Yuanfeng era of the Song dynasty (1078–1085), seven books were used for military instruction: Lü Wang's Six Secret Teachings (Liutao), the Sunzi, the Wuzi, the Methods of the Sima (Simafa), the Three Strategies (Sanlüe) of Huangshi, the Weiliaozi, and the Questions and Replies of Duke Wei Li (Li Weigong wendui). Chen Houshan [Chen Shidao 陳師道] said: "The Sunzi, Wuzi, and Methods of the Sima are perhaps ancient books; the Three Strategies of Huangshi and the Weiliaozi also have doubtful points; while the spuriousness and falsehood of the Six Secret Teachings and the Questions and Replies can be readily known." The Methods of the Sima states: "Ritual and law are exterior and interior to one another; the civil and the martial are left and right to one another." It also says: "If killing people brings peace to the people, killing them is permissible; if attacking a state is done out of love for its people, attacking it is permissible; if war is used to abolish war, even waging war is permissible." Is this not the governance of the former kings? As for the book of Wu Qi, it is close to the orthodox (zheng); the book of Sun Wu is wholly devoted to the unorthodox (qi). Wu's book esteems ritual and righteousness and clarifies instruction and training; Sun Wu's consists entirely of the Warring States arts of galloping into battle through deceit and force. When Marquis Wu [of Wei] floated down the West River, Wu Qi gave the reply that security "lies in virtue, not in strategic terrain." That being so, although these words of Wu Qi fall somewhat short when compared to the benevolence and righteousness of Tang and Wu, they have nothing to be ashamed of; and compared to those in the various states who discoursed on military affairs, they surpass them by far. text:
去病雖不學古兵法然其破匈奴亦豈無法乎
盖守法者兵家之常料敵者制勝之本宋高宗
謂有賢將有才將賢將以安社稷為心以尊朝
廷為重不專於戰勝攻取也才將以戰必勝為
事以攻必取為能而於安社稷尊朝廷之義則
或未之識也漢之鄧禹唐之李靖郭子儀輩非
賢將乎漢之韓信唐之尉遲敬德非才將乎今
之訓武欲其皆賢且才在擇將家之賢子弟教
之以詩書禮樂使聞仁義禮信之說然後習以
===

去病雖不學古兵法，然其破匈奴，亦豈無法乎？盖守法者，兵家之常；料敵者，制勝之本。宋高宗謂有賢將，有才將。賢將以安社稷為心，以尊朝廷為重，不專於戰勝攻取也；才將以戰必勝為事，以攻必取為能，而於安社稷、尊朝廷之義，則或未之識也。漢之鄧禹、唐之李靖、郭子儀輩，非賢將乎？漢之韓信、唐之尉遲敬德，非才將乎？今之訓武，欲其皆賢且才，在擇將家之賢子弟，教之以《詩》、《書》、禮、樂，使聞仁、義、禮、信之說，然後習以孫、吳兵法，則皆賢且才而名將出矣。用是以行師，則知所以安社稷、尊朝廷，戰必勝而攻必取矣。愚見如斯，執事先生幸恕其踈狂焉。

translation_en:
… Qubing 霍去病 did not study ancient military methods, yet when he defeated the Xiongnu 匈奴, how could he have been without a method? Indeed, adhering to methods is the constant norm of military strategists, while estimating the enemy is the foundation of securing victory. Emperor Gaozong of Song 宋高宗 said that there are worthy generals and there are talented generals. A worthy general takes securing the altars of soil and grain as his mind and honoring the court as his priority, not focusing exclusively on winning battles and capturing territory by assault. A talented general takes certain victory in battle as his business and certain capture in assault as his capability, yet as for the principles of securing the altars of soil and grain and honoring the court, perhaps he does not understand them. Were not Deng Yu 鄧禹 of the Han 漢 and men like Li Jing 李靖 and Guo Ziyi 郭子儀 of the Tang 唐 worthy generals? Were not Han Xin 韓信 of the Han and Yuchi Jingde 尉遲敬德 of the Tang talented generals? Today, in training military men, if we wish them all to be both worthy and talented, it lies in selecting worthy sons and younger brothers of military families, teaching them the Odes (Shi 詩), the Documents (Shu 書), rites, and music, making them hear the doctrines of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and trustworthiness, and afterward having them practice the military methods of Sun Wu 孫武 and Wu Qi 吳起; then all will be both worthy and talented, and renowned generals will emerge. Using such men to lead armies, they will know how to secure the altars of soil and grain and honor the court, and will certainly win when fighting and certainly capture when attacking. My humble view is thus; may you gentlemen in charge of the examination graciously pardon my crudeness and rashness.

Fifth Question
Liu Dingzhi 劉定之

對：自書契之作取於《夬》，而明决之理存；自書數之藝教於周，而變化之體滋。大而道德功業之顯著，以此而傳；小而名物度數之細微，以此而記。此明問之所以及也，請得言之。六書之義：一曰象形，則「日」、「月」之類，象其形體，圓而竒為「日」，闕而耦為「月」也；曰會意，則「武」、「信」之類，會合人意，止戈為「武」，人言為「信」也；曰轉注，則「老」、「考」之類，建類一首，而文意轉相注受；曰假借，則「令」、「長」之類，本為一字，借而兩用；曰諧聲，則「江」、「河」之類，以「水」為形，「工」、「可」為聲；曰處事，則「上」、「下」之類，人在「一」上、人在「一」下。其義如此。而書之變，則伏羲有龍書，神農有穗書，因所見而創也；題經目之有懸針書，刻印章之有剖符書，因所用而改也；史籀之大篆、

…it ought to be singled out and presented as an example.
Examiner and Academician Chen's comment: All three sessions are well-matched; he is a gentleman of literary learning.
Examiner and Vice Supervisor of the Household Wang's comment: His five policy essays are rich and accomplished, well matching his performance in the earlier sessions. Even on a minor matter like the study of script and characters, he has investigated it with such precision; from this, the rest can be known. He deserves to be placed at the very top of the list.
Reply: Ever since the creation of written documents and tallies was modeled on the hexagram Guai (Breakthrough), the principle of clear decision has been preserved; ever since the arts of writing and mathematics were taught in the Zhou dynasty, the forms of transformation have proliferated. In great matters, the manifest brilliance of moral virtue and meritorious achievement is transmitted through this; in small matters, the minute details of names, objects, standards, and numbers are recorded through this. This is why your enlightened question touches upon the subject; allow me to speak of it. As for the principles of the Six Categories of Script (liushu): First is "pictographs" (xiangxing), such as "sun" (ri 日) and "moon" (yue 月), which depict their physical forms—round and singular (yang) for the sun, crescent-shaped and paired (yin) for the moon. Next is "compound ideographs" (huiyi), such as "martial" (wu 武) and "trustworthy" (xin 信), which combine human concepts—to stay (zhi 止) the halberd (ge 戈) makes "martial," and a person's (ren 人) word (yan 言) makes "trustworthy." Next is "mutually explanatory characters" (zhuanzhu), such as "aged" (lao 老) and "elderly" (kao 考), which establish a category under a single heading while their graphic meanings turn and flow into one another. Next is "phonetic loan characters" (jiajie), such as "command/magistrate" (ling 令) and "long/senior" (zhang 長), where what is originally a single character is borrowed for a dual use. Next is "phono-semantic compounds" (xiesheng), such as "Yangtze River" (jiang 江) and "Yellow River" (he 河), which take "water" (shui 水) as their semantic form and gong (工) or ke (可) as their phonetic element. Next is "indicative characters" (chushi [zhishi]), such as "above" (shang 上) and "below" (xia 下), showing a person [mark] above the horizontal stroke "one" (yi 一) or a person [mark] below the horizontal stroke "one." Such are their principles. As for the transformations of script: Fuxi had the Dragon Script (longshu) and Shennong had the Grain-Ear Script (suishu), which were created on the basis of what they observed; there was the Suspended-Needle Script (xuanzhenshu) for inscribing the titles of classics, and the Split-Tally Script (poufushu) for carving seals, which were modified on the basis of how they were used; the Great Seal script (dazhuan) of Historian Zhou (Shizhou)…

title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
李斯之小篆因時而更程邈之隸書鍾繇之楷
法與日而精而書之變極矣若乃右軍之書人
猶謂之俗者何也盖黄庭遒勁蘭亭神助美則
美矣龍跳天門虎卧鳳閣壮則壮矣其於六書
之義何如哉此韓子所以歎也執事謂專古書
則不宜於用為今書則或謂之俗將何所取愚
竊謂書無古今人有古今以顔真卿之忠栁公
拳之直雖為今書亦何讓於古必若執事所云
則愚嘗聞徐鉉之意以為朝廷高文大冊勒之
===
金石宜用古書若夫日用之常則今書足矣此
其可行者也記曰德成而上藝成而下先儒嘗
謂一向好著亦自喪志故書雖不可不知而亦
不必泥也請以是復明問執事以為如何

拳之直雖為今書亦何讓於古必若執事所云
則愚甞聞徐鉉之意以為朝廷高文大用勒之
===
金石宜用古書若夫日用之常則今書足矣此
其可行者也記曰德成而上藝成而下先儒甞
謂一向好著亦自喪志故書雖不可不知而亦
不必泥也請以是復明問執事以為如何
punctuated: 李斯之小篆，因時而更；程邈之隸書、鍾繇之楷法，與日而精，而書之變極矣。若乃右軍之書，人猶謂之俗者，何也？盖《黄庭》遒勁、《蘭亭》神助，美則美矣；「龍跳天門，虎卧鳳閣」，壮則壮矣；其於六書之義何如哉？此韓子所以歎也。執事謂「專古書則不宜於用，為今書則或謂之俗，將何所取」，愚竊謂書無古今，人有古今。以顔真卿之忠、栁公拳之直，雖為今書，亦何讓於古？必若執事所云，則愚嘗聞徐鉉之意，以為朝廷高文大冊，勒之金石，宜用古書；若夫日用之常，則今書足矣。此其可行者也。《記》曰：「德成而上，藝成而下。」先儒嘗謂：「一向好著，亦自喪志。」故書雖不可不知，而亦不必泥也。請以是復明問，執事以為如何？
translation_en:
… and Li Si's 李斯 small seal script changed in response to the times; Cheng Miao's 程邈 clerical script and Zhong Yao's 鍾繇 regular script grew more refined by the day, and with them the transformations of calligraphy reached their limit. As for the calligraphy of the General of the Right Army [Wang Xizhi 王羲之], why is it that people still call it vulgar? Indeed, the Yellow Court Scripture (Huangting jing 黃庭經) is vigorous and forceful, and the Orchid Pavilion Preface (Lanting xu 蘭亭序) was aided by the divine—beautiful they certainly are; "dragons leaping at the Gate of Heaven, tigers crouching at the Phoenix Pavilion"—magnificent this certainly is; yet how do they stand with respect to the principles of the six scripts (liushu 六書)? This is why Master Han [Han Yu 韓愈] sighed.

When Your Excellency asks, "If one focuses exclusively on ancient scripts, they are unsuited for practical use; if one practices modern script, some call it vulgar—what then should one adopt?", I venture to say that in calligraphy there is no ancient or modern, whereas in men there is ancient and modern. With the loyalty of Yan Zhenqing 顏真卿 and the uprightness of Liu Gongquan 柳公權 [written 栁公拳], even though they wrote in the modern script, how do they yield anything to the ancients? If we must address what Your Excellency has stated, I have heard the view of Xu Xuan 徐鉉, who held that for the court's lofty compositions and grand charters, when engraved upon bronze and stone, it is fitting to use the ancient script; as for ordinary daily use, the modern script suffices. This is a practicable course.

The Record (Liji 禮記) says: "Those accomplished in virtue rank above; those accomplished in arts rank below." A former Confucian scholar [Cheng Hao 程顥] once said: "Being single-mindedly fond of it also saps one's moral resolve." Therefore, although calligraphy is something one cannot fail to understand, neither need one be bogged down in it. I beg to offer this in reply to your enlightened question; what does Your Excellency think?

title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
會試錄後序
皇上龍飛紀元之初實當論秀興賢之
歲於是天下俊秀承鄉薦而起者
咸以其學来會試于禮部此正萬
邦黎獻共惟帝臣雲從龍風從虎
聖人作而萬物覩之時也於乎盛哉尚
書臣淡侍郎臣敞臣士嘉既舉行其
典而臣直臣循奉
===
命為考試官乃相與簡其文之愈於
倫輩者百人得士之盛固先往昔
士之奮身遭
時亦鮮有能或之先也臣循竊惟為
國莫先於得賢得賢莫先於科目
是以
聖朝
祖宗漸仁摩義興學育材為往昔先

會試錄後序
皇上龍飛紀元之初，實當論秀興賢之歲。於是天下俊秀承鄉薦而起者，咸以其學来會試于禮部。此正萬邦黎獻共惟帝臣，雲從龍、風從虎，聖人作而萬物覩之時也。於乎盛哉！尚書臣淡、侍郎臣敞、臣士嘉既舉行其典，而臣直、臣循奉命為考試官，乃相與簡其文之愈於倫輩者百人。得士之盛，固先往昔；士之奮身遭時，亦鮮有能或之先也。臣循竊惟：為國莫先於得賢，得賢莫先於科目。是以聖朝祖宗漸仁摩義，興學育材，為往昔先；
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

The start of the inaugural reign year following His Majesty's ascension to the throne happens truly to coincide with the year for evaluating talents and promoting the worthy. Thereupon, the outstanding talents across the empire who have risen up bearing provincial recommendations have all come with their learning to take the Metropolitan Examination at the Ministry of Rites. This is truly the moment when "the multitudinous worthy men of the myriad states all wish to be the sovereign's subjects," when "clouds follow the dragon, winds follow the tiger, the sage arises and all things behold him." Oh, how magnificent! After the Minister, your servant [Hu] Dan 胡濙, and the Vice Ministers, your servants [Wang] Chang 王敞 and [Wu] Shijia 吾士嘉 [Wu Shen 吾紳], carried out the ceremony, your servants [Wang] Zhi 王直 and [陈] Xun 陳循 received the Imperial command to serve as Examiners, and together we selected one hundred men whose writings surpassed those of their peers. The flourishing abundance of scholars obtained certainly surpasses that of the past, and in these scholars' rousing themselves to meet with such an era, rarely has anyone ever been able to surpass them either. Your servant Xun humbly reflects that in governing the state, nothing takes precedence over obtaining worthy men, and in obtaining worthy men, nothing takes precedence over the examination system. Therefore, the Imperial Ancestors of our Sacred Dynasty imbued the realm with benevolence and honed it with righteousness, establishing schools and nurturing talents in a manner that surpassed the past; …

title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
皇上崇文好士簡賢選能為帝王先則
夫今日得士之先往昔豈無自而
然哉諸生抱負而来固皆懷先乎
人之志者也既得先乎人於鄉薦
與春闈之試矣其務所以先乎人
於
大廷之對有不待言雖然古之大賢
君子固未聞有懷先乎人之志者
===
也惟於教人則曰人一能之己百
之人十能之己千之又曰第一不
以遜與別人所以然者豈有他哉
愚欲其至於明柔欲其至於強士
欲其至於大賢耳果有人能用力
盡心如是而不懈焉則大賢之域
真可以至也至於大賢之域則其
先乎人也孰能禦之今諸生於所

也惟於教人則曰人一能之己百
之人十能之己千之又曰苐一不
以遜與別人所以然者豈有他哉

punctuated: 皇上崇文好士，簡賢選能，為帝王先，則夫今日得士之先往昔，豈無自而然哉？諸生抱負而来，固皆懷先乎人之志者也。既得先乎人於鄉薦與春闈之試矣，其務所以先乎人於大廷之對，有不待言。雖然，古之大賢君子，固未聞有懷先乎人之志者也。惟於教人，則曰：「人一能之，己百之；人十能之，己千之。」又曰：「第一不以遜與別人。」所以然者，豈有他哉？愚欲其至於明，柔欲其至於強，士欲其至於大賢耳。果有人能用力盡心如是而不懈焉，則大賢之域真可以至也。至於大賢之域，則其先乎人也，孰能禦之？今諸生於所
translation_en: … His Majesty reveres learning and cherishes scholars, selecting the worthy and choosing the capable, taking precedence over past emperors and kings. Thus, how could today's success in obtaining scholars surpassing that of the past come about without cause? The candidates have come bearing high ambitions, and naturally all harbor the aspiration to surpass others. Having already surpassed others in the Provincial Examination and the spring Metropolitan Examination, it goes without saying that they will strive to surpass others in their responses at the great court in the Palace Examination. Even so, among the great worthies and noble men of antiquity, one has never heard of any who harbored the aspiration merely to surpass others. Only in teaching people was it said: "If another succeeds by one effort, I will use a hundred; if another succeeds by ten, I will use a thousand." And it was also said: "Do not yield the first place to anyone else." Why was this so, if not simply because they wished the foolish to attain enlightenment, the weak to attain strength, and scholars to attain the status of great worthies? If indeed there is someone who can exert his strength and exhaust his mind in this way without slackening, then the realm of the great worthies can truly be reached. Once one reaches the realm of the great worthies, who could prevent him from surpassing others? Now, in what the candidates…

title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
學固亦加百倍之功不欲以遜與
別人無疑使惟施於進身之計以
求一先乎人而止豈大賢君子為
己之學哉大賢君子人皆可為者
也故曰有為者亦若是况遊聖賢
之門誦聖賢之書以為言而可不
由其道以為行乎凡預名茲選者
繼今所當百倍其功不以遜與別
===
人顧不在勉其在己耶持身必勉
以敦行先居官必勉以敬事先以
至於盡堯舜吾
君堯舜吾民之道皆當勉其所以先乎
人者而又隨事究所當務無不然
焉庶幾不愧以科第先乎人而為
大賢君子之歸矣若然雖公卿宰
輔皆由此選其亦宜也小錄之成

punctuated: 學，固亦加百倍之功，不欲以遜與別人無疑。使惟施於進身之計，以求一先乎人而止，豈大賢君子為己之學哉？大賢君子，人皆可為者也，故曰：「有為者亦若是。」况遊聖賢之門，誦聖賢之書以為言，而可不由其道以為行乎？凡預名茲選者，繼今所當百倍其功、不以遜與別人，顧不在勉其在己耶？持身必勉以敦行先，居官必勉以敬事先，以至於盡堯舜吾君、堯舜吾民之道，皆當勉其所以先乎人者，而又隨事究所當務，無不然焉，庶幾不愧以科第先乎人，而為大賢君子之歸矣。若然，雖公卿宰輔皆由此選，其亦宜也。小錄之成，
translation_en: … studies, you have indeed redoubled your efforts a hundredfold, undoubtedly unwilling to yield first place to others. Yet if this effort were applied solely as a means of personal advancement—merely to surpass others once and stop there—how could that be the learning for oneself of a great worthy or noble man? Anyone can become a great worthy or a noble man; hence it is said, "Those who would achieve something are also like this." How much more so for those who roam within the gates of the sages and worthies and recite their books to form their own words—how could they not also follow their Way in their conduct? For all whose names are included in this selection, from this day forward, where you ought to redouble your efforts a hundredfold and refuse to yield to others—does this not lie in striving to cultivate what is within yourselves? In conducting yourselves, you must strive to put earnest conduct first; in holding office, you must strive to put reverence for your duties first; and even up to fulfilling the Way of making our sovereign like Yao and Shun and our people like those of Yao and Shun, in all things you ought to strive to surpass others, while investigating what is required in every matter without exception. In this way, you may perhaps feel no shame in having surpassed others through the examination ranks, and truly arrive at the stature of great worthies and noble men. If so, even if Dukes, Ministers, and Chief Councilors are all drawn from this selection, it will indeed be fitting. Now that this brief record is completed, …

title: 正統元年會試錄
text:
循旣濫預文衡敢以蕪陋而不為
諸生言之乎然非一人私勸而實
國家所期望者勉之勉之
行在翰林院侍講學士奉直大
夫陳循謹序

循旣濫預文衡，敢以蕪陋而不為諸生言之乎？然非一人私勸，而實國家所期望者。勉之！勉之！
行在翰林院侍講學士、奉直大夫陳循謹序。
translation_en:
… Since I, Xun, have unworthily participated in judging the literary compositions, how dare I refrain from speaking of this to the scholars on account of my own crudeness and inadequacy? Yet this is not merely the private exhortation of one individual, but in truth what the State expects of you. Strive at it! Strive at it!
Respectfully prefaced by Chen Xun 陳循, Academician Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy in the Auxiliary Administration, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel.
